chapters.markdown:
# Economic Growth versus Economic Development

## 1. Growth and development

- **Economic growth:** increase in real output/income over time; mainly quantitative. **Growth rate = [(real GDP this year − real GDP last year) / real GDP last year] × 100.** Use comparable constant-price data.
- **Economic development:** broader improvement in living standards, capabilities and opportunities, alongside economic/structural change; includes poverty, jobs, distribution, health, education and gender equity.
- **Growth indicators:** real GDP/GNP growth, real per-capita income. **Development indicators:** HDI/IHDI, gender indices, poverty and wellbeing measures.
- Growth increases resources; **jobs, fair opportunities and effective public services** help translate them into development. Higher income alone does not ensure shared benefits.
- **Corrections:** growth can be long-term; development can be quantified through indicators, though no single number captures it fully. Both concepts matter in developed and developing countries.
- Human development enlarges choices, capabilities and freedoms. Four pillars associated with **Mahbub ul Haq:** equity, sustainability, productivity and empowerment. Amartya Sen's capability approach emphasises people's real freedom to live lives they value.

![Growth supports development when people can participate and benefit.](Revision%20Diagrams/growth.svg)

*Growth supports development when people can participate and benefit.*

## 2. Drivers, obstacles and remedies

- **Resources/production:** natural resources, capital formation, agricultural surplus/productivity, structural transformation and an efficient financial system.
- **People/institutions:** human capital; education, skills and technology; health; effective law/order; ethical/social values and good governance. These overlap with economic factors—the book's two-way grouping is not a rigid separation.
- **Population pressure relative to resources →** education, health, productive employment and infrastructure; population can become a demographic dividend when skills/jobs exist.
- **Agriculture dependence/disguised unemployment →** modern technology, higher productivity, diversification and non-farm jobs.
- **Low income/inequality/unemployment/skill mismatch →** labour-intensive employment, inclusion, quality education and skills; implement NEP effectively.
- **Infrastructure/finance gaps →** investment, wider banking access and resolution of non-performing assets (NPAs).
- **Corruption/misdirected priorities →** transparency, accountability and accessible digital processes.
- **Poor health/resource depletion →** better health spending and welfare delivery; sustainable resource use.
- **Underdevelopment:** low per-capita income, capital formation and labour productivity; widespread poverty/inequality; unemployment/underemployment; weak human capital and high dependence on primary-sector employment. It is multidimensional, not an income label alone.

## 3. Inclusive growth

- **Meaning:** broad participation in growth and fair access to its benefits, across income, gender, caste, religion and region. Inclusion requires opportunities and capabilities, not only redistribution after growth.
- **Vertical inequality:** between people at different income levels. **Horizontal inequality:** between groups, e.g. gender/social groups. Also address regional disparities.
- Goals: poverty reduction, productive jobs, opportunities across all sectors, smaller gaps between advantaged/disadvantaged groups. “Balanced sectors” does not mean identical sectoral growth rates.
- India's obstacles: poverty, weak job creation, skills mismatch, agricultural productivity gaps, social barriers, regional disparities, inequality and governance weaknesses.
- **Global MPI 2025:** India's latest survey used is **2019–21**; incidence **16.4%**, approximately **235.74 million** poor using 2023 population. A 2025 report date is not a 2025 survey. [UNDP country profile](https://hdr.undp.org/sites/default/files/Country-Profiles/MPI2025/IND.pdf)
- **415 million** exited multidimensional poverty during **2005–06 to 2019–21** in the global MPI comparison. Do not mix this with national-MPI estimates or shorter periods. [UNDP](https://www.undp.org/turkiye/press-releases/25-countries-halved-multidimensional-poverty-within-15-years-11-billion-remain-poor)
- **Inclusive Development Index, WEF (2018):** growth/development; inclusion; intergenerational equity/sustainability. Covered 103 economies in two groups; India **62nd of 74 emerging economies**. Historical rank, not a current league table. [WEF](https://www.weforum.org/press/2018/01/focus-on-gdp-fuelling-inequality-and-short-termism/)

![Inclusive growth needs access, participation and shared gains.](Revision%20Diagrams/inclusion.svg)

*Inclusive growth needs access, participation and shared gains.*

## 4. Composite Development Index of States

- **Raghuram Rajan Committee, 2013:** proposed a composite (under)development index for States and a funds-allocation framework considering need and performance. [Committee release](https://www.pib.gov.in/newsite/erelcontent.aspx?lang=2&reg=48&relid=99675)
- **Ten equally weighted components:** monthly per-capita consumption expenditure; education; health; household amenities; poverty; female literacy; SC/ST population share; urbanisation; financial inclusion; connectivity.
- This is distinct from UNDP's HDI and WEF's Inclusive Development Index. A deprivation/underdevelopment score should not be interpreted like an achievement score.

## 5. HDI: health + education + income

- **Publisher:** UNDP, within the Human Development Report, first issued **1990**. HDI summarises average achievement; the report also includes IHDI, GDI, GII and MPI.
- **Health:** life expectancy at birth. **Education:** expected years of schooling for a school-entry-age child and mean years of schooling for adults **25+**. **Living standard:** GNI per capita in **PPP dollars**, not GDP per capita.
- **HDI = (health index × education index × income index)^(1/3):** geometric mean of three normalised dimension indices. Values range from 0 to 1; higher is better.
- **Categories:** very high **≥0.800**; high **0.700–0.799**; medium **0.550–0.699**; low **<0.550**.
- Equal GNI per capita can yield different human-development outcomes due to policy, distribution and public services. HDI is broader than income, but still hides inequalities and does not capture every freedom or environmental cost.

![Remember H–E–I: health, education, income. These are three dimensions, four underlying indicators.](Revision%20Diagrams/hdi.svg)

*Remember H–E–I: health, education, income. These are three dimensions, four underlying indicators.*

## 6. HDI, IHDI and planetary pressures

- **HDI:** average achievements. **IHDI:** discounts the same health/education/income dimensions for inequality in their distribution; introduced **2010**. Inequality is not a new fourth HDI dimension.
- **IHDI ≤ HDI**; equality gives IHDI = HDI. **Loss due to inequality = (1 − IHDI/HDI) × 100.**
- **HDR 2025, mainly 2023 data:** India HDI **0.685**, rank **130/193**, medium category; IHDI **0.475**, loss **30.7%**. The book incorrectly calls 0.475 “HDI”.
- India indicators: life expectancy **72.0 years**; mean schooling **6.88 years**; expected schooling **12.95 years**; GNI/person **$9,046.76, 2021 PPP**. [UNDP India](https://www.undp.org/india/press-releases/indias-human-development-continues-make-progress-ranks-130-out-193-countries)
- Consistent 2025-report series: 2022 HDI **0.676 → 0.685 in 2023**. The older HDR2023/24 publication reported 0.644 for 2022; revisions mean these editions should not be treated as a directly comparable unrevised series. Expected schooling was **12.96 → 12.95**, so not every indicator increased.
- Official HDR2025 dimension-inequality figures: health **15.5%**, education **36.9%**, income **37.4%**; these replace the book's mixed-vintage values. [HDR tables 1–3](https://report.hdr.undp.org/assets/pdfs/UNDP%20HDR%20-%20A%20Matter%20of%20Choice%20-%20Full%20Report.pdf)
- **HDR2025 ranks:** Iceland **1 (0.972)**; Norway/Switzerland **2 (0.970)**; Denmark **4 (0.962)**; South Sudan **193 (0.388)**. Neighbours: China **78**, Sri Lanka **89**, Bhutan **125**, India/Bangladesh **130**, Nepal **145**, Pakistan **168**, Afghanistan **181**. Corrected Bhutan/China ranks replace the book's 127/75. [HDR](https://report.hdr.undp.org/assets/pdfs/UNDP%20HDR%20-%20A%20Matter%20of%20Choice%20-%20Full%20Report.pdf)
- **Report title, 2025:** “A Matter of Choice: People and Possibilities in the Age of AI”.
- **PHDI, introduced 2020:** adjusts HDI for **per-capita CO₂ emissions and material footprint**; achievements with less planetary pressure are favoured. It complements rather than replaces HDI.

![HDR2025 figures: higher average achievement does not guarantee equally shared achievement.](Revision%20Diagrams/ihdi.svg)

*HDR2025 figures: higher average achievement does not guarantee equally shared achievement.*

## 7. GII and GDI: do not interchange

- **GII—Gender Inequality Index (UNDP; 2010):** disadvantage in **reproductive health, empowerment and labour-market participation**. **0 = no measured inequality; 1 = maximum**; lower is better.
- Health indicators: maternal mortality and adolescent births. Empowerment: parliamentary representation and secondary education. Labour: female/male labour-force participation.
- **HDR2025:** India GII **0.403**, rank **102/172**; world **0.455**, South Asia **0.458**. Adolescent births **14.1 per 1,000 women aged 15–19**; LFPR, ages 15+: women **35.1%**, men **76.4%**, gap **41.3 percentage points**. These replace the older 0.419/15.7/28.9% figures mixed into the book. Reference years vary by component. [HDR table 5](https://report.hdr.undp.org/assets/pdfs/UNDP%20HDR%20-%20A%20Matter%20of%20Choice%20-%20Full%20Report.pdf)
- **GDI—Gender Development Index (UNDP): GDI = female HDI / male HDI.** Same three HDI dimensions; education includes both mean and expected schooling. A value closer to **1** means greater parity; GDI can exceed 1.
- **HDR2025, 2023 data:** GDI **0.874**; female HDI **0.631**, male **0.722**. Female/male life expectancy **73.6/70.5 years**; mean schooling **5.8/8.0**; expected schooling **13.0/12.9**; GNI/person **$4,543/$13,273 (2021 PPP)**. The book's 0.865 and 0.616/0.712 use older figures; they are not current HDR2025 values. [HDR table 4](https://report.hdr.undp.org/assets/pdfs/UNDP%20HDR%20-%20A%20Matter%20of%20Choice%20-%20Full%20Report.pdf)

## 8. Global Gender Gap Index

- **Publisher:** World Economic Forum; first introduced **2006**. Measures gender parity, not simply absolute development levels.
- Four subindices: **economic participation/opportunity; educational attainment; health/survival; political empowerment**.
- **0–1:** higher score means more of the gap closed; 1 is the parity benchmark. This direction is opposite to GII.
- **2025:** India **131/148**, score **0.644**; Iceland **0.926**, followed by Finland, Norway and the UK. World score **68.8%**; the matched-country comparison improved by about **0.3 percentage points**. [WEF2025](https://www.weforum.org/publications/global-gender-gap-report-2025/in-full/benchmarking-gender-gaps-2025/)
- **2026 update:** India retains rank **131**, score **0.645** (64.5% parity). Keep this separate from the 2025 edition. [WEF2026](https://www.weforum.org/publications/global-gender-gap-report-2026/in-full/benchmarking-gender-gaps-2026/)

## 9. World Happiness Report

- First published **2012**. Published by Oxford's **Wellbeing Research Centre**, in partnership with **Gallup, the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network and an independent editorial board**; attributing publication solely to SDSN is incomplete. [About the report](https://files.worldhappiness.report/WHR26_Statistical_Appendix.pdfabout)
- **Ranking:** average self-reported life evaluations on the **Cantril ladder, 0–10**, using Gallup World Poll data, normally averaged over three years. It is **not** a weighted index of six inputs.
- Six factors used to **explain** differences: GDP/person (PPP); social support; healthy life expectancy; freedom to choose; generosity; perceived corruption. [Methodology FAQ](https://files.worldhappiness.report/WHR26_Statistical_Appendix.pdffaq)
- **2026:** India **116/147**, score **4.536**; book's previous score **4.389** refers to the older edition. Finland first for the **ninth consecutive year**, then **Iceland and Denmark** (the book reverses these two). Afghanistan last; Sierra Leone second-last; Lebanon also near the bottom. [2026 rankings](https://files.worldhappiness.report/WHR26_Statistical_Appendix.pdf)
- Report focus: **Happiness and Social Media (2026)**; **Caring and Sharing (2025)**. India's social support and freedom are useful policy lenses, but avoid assigning a cause to a rank without evidence. [2026 report](https://files.worldhappiness.report/WHR26_Statistical_Appendix.pdf26)
- **International Day of Happiness: 20 March.** A report's theme should not automatically be labelled the UN observance's official theme.

## 10. Gross National Happiness

- **Bhutan:** associated with fourth King **Jigme Singye Wangchuck**, 1970s; holistic progress gives importance to non-economic wellbeing.
- **Four pillars:** sustainable/equitable socio-economic development; good governance; cultural preservation; environmental conservation.
- **GNH Index:** **33 indicators, nine domains**—psychological wellbeing, health, education, time use, cultural diversity/resilience, good governance, community vitality, ecological diversity/resilience and living standards. [Bhutan consulate](https://bhutan-hcg.org/en/about-bhutan/culture/gnh/)
- **GNH ≠ World Happiness Report:** a multidimensional Bhutanese framework versus international self-reported life-evaluation rankings.
- **Delhi Happiness Curriculum, 2018:** mindfulness/attention, critical thinking/reflection, social-emotional skills and confident, responsible personalities. [SCERT](https://scert.delhi.gov.in/scert/happiness-curriculum-chvtl)
- Chapter's Indian example: **Madhya Pradesh's Happiness Department/Anand Sansthan, 2016**. The book also names Andhra Pradesh as a subsequent adopter; treat the “second State” chronology as its claim, not an independently established ranking.

## 11. Sustainability and country classification

- **Sustainable development:** improve present wellbeing without undermining future generations' ability to meet needs. Inclusion concerns who benefits now; sustainability also concerns future people and environmental limits.
- **Sustainable Development Report:** SDSN's SDG Index/Dashboards assess progress towards the **17 SDGs**; separate from HDI and from the UN's own SDG progress reporting. **2026 India: rank **94**, score **68.33**/100**. [SDSN report](https://sdgtransformationcenter.org/reports/sustainable-development-report-2026), [rankings](https://dashboards.sdgindex.org/rankings/)
- **World Bank:** classifies economies by **GNI/person, Atlas method**; this is not PPP and not a sector-based classification. Thresholds are updated annually on **1 July**.
- **FY2027 (July 2026–June 2027), 2025 GNI:** low **≤$1,175**; lower-middle **$1,176–4,635**; upper-middle **$4,636–14,375**; high **>$14,375**. India lower-middle; China upper-middle; USA high. The book's $1,005/$3,995/$12,235 thresholds are outdated and its ranges contain inconsistencies. [World Bank](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519-world-bank-country-and-lending-groups)
- **Developed/developing:** broad structural labels involving industrialisation, technology, institutions and living standards; not exact synonyms for World Bank income classes. A developing economy need not be dominated by agriculture.
- **Least Developed Countries (UN category):** severe structural constraints, low income, weak human assets and vulnerability to economic/environmental shocks. Income, human assets and vulnerability all matter; Somalia and Sudan are examples cited in the chapter.

## 12. Prelims PYQs: recall

- **2018 human-capital formation → (c), 2 and 4 only:** knowledge, skills and capacities; intangible wealth, not merely tangible assets or financial capital.
- **2013 growth in country X → (c), capital formation:** the supplied key identifies additions to productive capital. In real economies, efficient use and demand also matter; do not turn the question into an unconditional guarantee.
- **2012 inclusive governance → (c), 2, 3 and 4 only:** effective District Planning Committees, public-health spending and Mid-day Meals. Simply permitting NBFCs to do banking does not by itself establish inclusive governance.

## 13. Mains PYQs: answer cues

- **2025 HDI versus IHDI, India:** average versus distribution-adjusted achievement → India **0.685/0.475** and **30.7%** loss → explain why shared health, education and income achievements better reflect inclusion; IHDI still does not capture every dimension.
- **2022 inclusive growth in a market economy/financial inclusion:** markets create opportunities, but exclusion/market failures need public action. Savings, payments, responsible credit and insurance support enterprise/resilience; access alone is insufficient without affordability, capability and consumer protection.
- **2019 inclusion and sustainability together:** jobs/services and equity today + conservation, resilient infrastructure and intergenerational equity; manage trade-offs through a just transition.
- **2017 salient features/India/measures:** participation, opportunity, jobs, reduced poverty/group/regional gaps → balanced evidence → human capital, agriculture/MSMEs, finance, social protection and governance. This PYQ also relates to National Income.
- **2016 manpower-related challenges:** interpret through skill mismatch, low productivity, unemployment, job quality and demographic pressures; suggest training, health/education, labour-intensive opportunities and better matching, rather than labelling people as inherently unproductive.

## 14. One-minute recall

- **Growth:** more real output. **Development:** better lives/capabilities. **Inclusion:** who participates/benefits. **Sustainability:** whether benefits endure.
- **HDI:** health + education + GNI. **IHDI:** same dimensions, inequality discount. **PHDI:** planetary-pressure adjustment.
- **GDI:** female/male HDI, parity near 1. **GII:** inequality, lower better. **WEF gender gap:** parity, higher better.
- **WHR:** reported life evaluation; six variables explain it. **GNH:** Bhutan's 4 pillars/9 domains/33 indicators.
- **Income groups:** World Bank, GNI/person, Atlas method; annual thresholds. **LDC:** separate UN structural category.
- **Rank ≠ score; report year ≠ data year.** Check edition, survey period, units and publisher before comparing.

Economic Growth versus Economic Development

1. Growth and development

  • Economic growth: increase in real output/income over time; mainly quantitative. Growth rate = [(real GDP this year − real GDP last year) / real GDP last year] × 100. Use comparable constant-price data.
  • Economic development: broader improvement in living standards, capabilities and opportunities, alongside economic/structural change; includes poverty, jobs, distribution, health, education and gender equity.
  • Growth indicators: real GDP/GNP growth, real per-capita income. Development indicators: HDI/IHDI, gender indices, poverty and wellbeing measures.
  • Growth increases resources; jobs, fair opportunities and effective public services help translate them into development. Higher income alone does not ensure shared benefits.
  • Corrections: growth can be long-term; development can be quantified through indicators, though no single number captures it fully. Both concepts matter in developed and developing countries.
  • Human development enlarges choices, capabilities and freedoms. Four pillars associated with Mahbub ul Haq: equity, sustainability, productivity and empowerment. Amartya Sen's capability approach emphasises people's real freedom to live lives they value.

2. Drivers, obstacles and remedies

  • Resources/production: natural resources, capital formation, agricultural surplus/productivity, structural transformation and an efficient financial system.
  • People/institutions: human capital; education, skills and technology; health; effective law/order; ethical/social values and good governance. These overlap with economic factors—the book's two-way grouping is not a rigid separation.
  • Population pressure relative to resources → education, health, productive employment and infrastructure; population can become a demographic dividend when skills/jobs exist.
  • Agriculture dependence/disguised unemployment → modern technology, higher productivity, diversification and non-farm jobs.
  • Low income/inequality/unemployment/skill mismatch → labour-intensive employment, inclusion, quality education and skills; implement NEP effectively.
  • Infrastructure/finance gaps → investment, wider banking access and resolution of non-performing assets (NPAs).
  • Corruption/misdirected priorities → transparency, accountability and accessible digital processes.
  • Poor health/resource depletion → better health spending and welfare delivery; sustainable resource use.

chapters.markdown:
# Money and Money Supply

## 1. Money: meaning, functions and qualities

- **Money:** anything generally accepted as payment for goods/services and settlement of debts. Legal recognition is important for currency, but **all money is not legal tender**: bank deposits also function as money.
- **Medium of exchange:** removes barter's double coincidence of wants; sell wheat for money, then buy rice.
- **Unit of account:** common measure for prices, accounting and comparison.
- **Store of value:** transfers purchasing power across time; inflation erodes its real value. Keynes emphasised holding money as an asset; avoid the absolute claim that earlier economists never recognised this function.
- **Standard of deferred payment:** denominates future obligations, enabling credit and contracts.
- **Six desirable qualities:** acceptability, portability, durability, divisibility, uniformity and controlled scarcity. A payment card is a means of accessing money, not a separate currency.

![Money performs four complementary functions.](Revision%20Diagrams/functions.svg)

*Money performs four complementary functions.*

## 2. Types of money: distinguish the basis

- **Commodity money:** a commodity itself used as money, e.g. gold. **Metallic money:** coins made of metals. **Paper money:** notes; these describe material, not necessarily backing.
- **Full-bodied money:** commodity/intrinsic value approximately equals face value. **Token money:** intrinsic value below face value.
- **Representative money:** redeemable claim on a backing commodity; representative full-bodied money has equivalent bullion backing held by the issuer. Modern Indian notes are not promises to deliver gold.
- **Fiat money:** value rests on legal authority, public confidence and acceptance, without commodity convertibility. “Non-commodity-backed” and “government-backed” describe its features, not two separate types. Market purchasing power is not fixed by government decree alone.
- **Fiduciary/optional money:** accepted on trust/agreement, e.g. cheques or bills of exchange; a creditor need not accept these as legal tender. A cheque instructs a deposit transfer; it is not an additional stock of money.
- **Commercial-bank money:** deposit balances usable for payment, created partly through lending. **Actual money:** general textbook label for money used in exchange. **Standard money:** recognised currency/unit of account; do not confuse this with the intrinsic-value test for full-bodied money.
- **Near money:** liquid assets readily convertible into transaction money, e.g. treasury bills, certificates of deposit and short-term deposits. Classification depends on the aggregate: savings-bank deposits may already count as money; they are not universally “outside money”.

## 3. Legal tender and currency issuance in India

- **Legal tender:** legally valid means of discharging a monetary debt, subject to applicable limits. **Unlimited:** no aggregate payment ceiling for valid notes; **limited:** statutory transaction ceiling for coins.
- **RBI issues banknotes; Government of India issues coins and ₹1 notes.** RBI distributes coins. RBI notes are Central-Government-guaranteed; ₹1 notes/coins are government liabilities. Banknotes carry the RBI Governor's signature; ₹1 notes carry the Finance Secretary's.
- **Coin limits per transaction:** denominations **₹1 and above: ₹1,000**; **50 paise: ₹10**. Voluntary acceptance above these limits is possible; coin deposits into bank accounts are a different matter.
- **₹2,000 notes:** withdrawal from circulation announced in **2023**, but they **continue as legal tender**. Withdrawal from circulation and demonetisation are different. [RBI currency FAQ](https://www.rbi.org.in/scripts/FAQView.aspx?Id=136)
- **2016 demonetisation:** old-series ₹500/₹1,000 notes lost legal-tender status from midnight **8 November 2016**. New-series ₹500 notes are valid.
- **RBI Act, 1934:** Section **22**—banknote issuance; **26**—legal tender/guarantee; **33**—Issue Department assets. The printed promise is a currency obligation, not gold convertibility.
- **Seigniorage:** economic benefit from issuing money. Face value minus production cost is a simplified illustration; RBI does not book every newly printed note's face value as profit. Currency is a liability; earnings on backing assets, costs and provisioning affect surplus transferred to government.

## 4. Money demand: Keynes's liquidity preference

- **Demand for money:** desired holdings of liquid purchasing power; distinct from demand for income or loans. Influenced by income, prices, interest/opportunity cost and expectations.
- **Transactions motive:** routine household/business payments. Higher real activity/income or prices generally increases nominal cash requirements; payment frequency and digital arrangements also matter.
- **Precautionary motive:** emergencies and unforeseen opportunities; normally rises with income and uncertainty. Transactions + precautionary holdings are **active cash balances**.
- **Speculative motive:** holding money rather than bonds because of expected returns/capital losses; linked to the store-of-value function. Generally **interest rate ↑ → money demand ↓**.
- **Bond price and yield move inversely:** low current rates may lead people to expect future rate increases and bond-price falls, encouraging cash holdings.
- **Liquidity trap:** at very low rates, additional liquidity may be willingly held rather than used for spending; conventional rate cuts become less effective. It has no universal “3%” threshold. Expectations, weak demand and balance-sheet problems matter.

![T–P–S: transactions, precautionary and speculative motives.](Revision%20Diagrams/demand.svg)

*T–P–S: transactions, precautionary and speculative motives.*

## 5. Money supply: stock, sources and determinants

- **Money supply:** stock of monetary assets held by the public at a point in time. It is a **stock**, unlike annual income/GDP, which is a **flow**.
- “Public” excludes the money-producing banking system and relevant government holdings. **Deposits owed by banks to the public count; banks' own cash/interbank balances are not public money.** Reserve money separately includes bank reserves.
- **RBI:** supplies currency/reserves and influences liquidity through policy rates, reserve requirements, securities and foreign-exchange operations. **Banks:** create deposit money when lending or buying assets from non-banks.
- **Loan → deposit creation; repayment of loan principal → deposit destruction.** Lending is constrained by capital, liquidity, regulation, borrower demand and credit risk—not an unlimited mechanical process.
- **Determinants:** reserve requirements, central-bank operations, banks' lending decisions, public currency preference, business cycle, financial inclusion/payment innovation, government financing and external flows.
- Booms often support credit/deposit growth; recessions can weaken it, but this is not an unavoidable rule. Financial innovation may change how aggregates are measured.
- **Velocity changes spending per unit of money; it does not itself mechanically create additional money stock.** Government borrowing/spending does not automatically increase broad money: financing source and subsequent transactions matter.

![Loan creation expands deposit money; principal repayment reverses it.](Revision%20Diagrams/creation.svg)

*Loan creation expands deposit money; principal repayment reverses it.*

## 6. Conventional monetary aggregates

- **C = currency with the public; DD = demand deposits with banks; OD = other deposits with RBI; TD = time deposits with banks.** Currency with the public = currency in circulation minus banks' cash holdings.
- **M₀ (reserve/base/high-powered money) = currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI.** Bank reserves make M₀ different from public money.
- **M₁ (narrow money) = C + DD + OD.** The chapter's table omits OD; include it.
- **M₂ = M₁ + savings deposits with post-office savings banks.**
- **M₃ (broad money) = M₁ + TD.** Main broad-money measure used in India.
- **M₄ = M₃ + all post-office savings-bank deposits, excluding National Savings Certificates.**
- **M₂ and M₃ are different additions to M₁:** they are not simply successive nested steps. Moving to broader aggregates generally adds less-liquid assets; do not treat **M₀ > M₁ > M₂ > M₃ > M₄** as a universal size or liquidity ranking. [RBI definitions](https://www.rbi.org.in/scripts/PublicationsView.aspx?Id=22715)

![M₂ and M₃ add different deposit categories to M₁.](Revision%20Diagrams/aggregates.svg)

*M₂ and M₃ add different deposit categories to M₁.*

## 7. New monetary and liquidity aggregates

- **1998 Working Group:** added aggregates using residency and maturity distinctions. Conventional M₁–M₄ did not simply disappear; distinguish new **NM** definitions from conventional measures.
- **NM₀ = M₀; NM₁ = C + DD + OD.** Demand/current deposits should not be double-counted.
- **NM₂ = NM₁ + residents' short-term time deposits**, contractual maturity **up to and including 1 year**.
- **NM₃ = NM₂ + residents' long-term time deposits + banks' call/term funding from financial institutions.** Residency treatment excludes specified non-resident foreign-currency repatriable deposits from NM₂/NM₃; do not equate every non-resident deposit category. [RBI guide](https://dbieold.rbi.org.in/DBIE/doc/Comprehensive%20Guide%20for%20Monthly%20Bulletin.pdf)
- **L₁ = NM₃ + all post-office savings-bank deposits**, excluding NSCs.
- **L₂ = L₁ + term deposits with term-lending/refinancing institutions + term borrowings by financial institutions + CDs issued by financial institutions.**
- **L₃ = L₂ + public deposits of NBFCs.** These extend measurement beyond banks; post-office deposits are included in L₁, contrary to the chapter's introductory exclusion claim. [RBI liquidity definitions](https://rbi.org.in/scripts/AnnualReportPublications.aspx?Id=896)
- **Publication rhythm described in the chapter:** M₀ weekly; M₁/M₃ fortnightly; L₁/L₂ monthly; L₃ quarterly. These are series conventions, not a promise that every release arrives at that interval.

## 8. Money multiplier and velocity

- **Observed money multiplier = M₃ / M₀.** If M₃ = ₹600 and M₀ = ₹100, multiplier = **6**. A rise in M₃ raises the ratio only if M₀ does not rise proportionately or faster.
- **Simple textbook deposit multiplier = 1/r**, where r is a reserve ratio; assumes full lending/redepositing, no currency leakage and no excess reserves. It is not identical to the observed M₃/M₀ ratio.
- With public currency preference **c = C/D** and bank reserve ratio **r = R/D**, a simplified multiplier is **(1+c)/(r+c)**. Higher currency leakage/excess reserves generally lowers it; stronger banking habits generally raise it.
- Higher CRR reduces lendable resources; SLR can constrain lending but cannot simply be added into every multiplier formula. Financial inclusion encourages deposit use. Loan demand, capital constraints and risk affect realised credit expansion.
- **Historical chapter claim:** multiplier rose broadly from the mid-1990s to 2016–17 and weakened thereafter, including 2019–20 to 2022–23. Treat this as period-specific, not a perpetual trend; neither every RBI deposit nor reverse-repo placement is mechanically identical to required reserves.
- **Velocity V = nominal GDP / chosen money stock M; MV = PY**, where PY is nominal output. If GDP = ₹1,000 and M = ₹200, **V = 5 per year**. Use consistent period/stock convention and state the chosen aggregate.
- Velocity reflects payment frequency, income/spending patterns, confidence, interest rates, credit/EMIs, financial inclusion, innovation and uncertainty. Development or EMI use does not guarantee a rise. Low-income households may spend receipts quickly, but economy-wide velocity is not inferred from that alone.
- **Multiplier:** broad-money stock per unit of monetary base. **Velocity:** nominal spending/output per unit of money over time. GDP cannot be controlled through money supply alone when velocity/real output change.

## 9. How monetary expansion works

- **RBI buys government securities → bank reserves/liquidity rise.** Sale normally absorbs liquidity. Broad-money effects depend partly on whether the counterparty is a bank or non-bank.
- **RBI buys foreign exchange → injects rupee liquidity**; sale normally absorbs it. **Sterilisation** through offsetting operations can neutralise the liquidity effect.
- Lower reserve requirements can support lending; actual credit expansion depends on demand and bank constraints. Government financing through bank/central-bank transactions can affect deposits/reserves; borrowing from existing private savings is not automatically money creation.
- **PYQ trap:** with money supply fixed, greater money demand tends to **raise interest rates** in the standard liquidity-preference model.

## 10. Indian currency: history and banknote facts

- **INR; ₹; ₹1 = 100 paise.** Symbol combines Devanagari “र” and Roman “R”, with two horizontal strokes.
- **1861 Paper Currency Act:** government monopoly of note issue replaced private/presidency-bank issuance; James Wilson was associated with early paper-currency reform. **RBI began operations 1 April 1935.** ₹1 notes were reintroduced in **1940**; the chapter says August, while RBI records issuance since **July 1940**. [RBI currency history](https://rbi.org.in/scripts/PublicationsView.aspx?Id=18086)
- **₹10,000:** highest denomination historically printed; introduced **1938**, demonetised **1946**, reintroduced **1954**, demonetised again **1978**.
- **1949 ₹1 note:** first note of independent India; Lion Capital at Sarnath replaced the British monarch's portrait. **1970:** “Satyameva Jayate” introduced. **October 1987:** ₹500 with Gandhi portrait and Ashoka Pillar watermark.
- **Languages:** 15 in the language panel plus Hindi and English = **17**. Paper is cotton-based. Equal serial numbers can occur with differing inset letter, printing year or Governor's signature; some notes have no inset letter.
- **2011:** non-sequential numbering introduced for efficiency. **Star series:** an asterisk identifies replacement notes in packets; it does not invalidate a note.
- Currency backing includes eligible assets under Section 33, such as gold, government securities and foreign securities; **asset backing ≠ commodity convertibility**.
- **MANI (Mobile Aided Note Identifier):** launched **1 January 2020** for visually impaired users; identifies denominations through audio. Hindi/English plus 11 additional languages are described in the chapter: Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu and Urdu. Denomination recognition does not establish authenticity.

## 11. Banknote series and motifs

- **Ashoka Pillar series:** Lion Capital imagery. **Mahatma Gandhi series, 1996:** Gandhi portrait on front; Lion Capital retained elsewhere, with Gandhi watermark.
- **MG 2005 security upgrade:** ₹50/₹100—August 2005; ₹500/₹1,000—October 2005; ₹10—April 2006; ₹20—August 2006. Old ₹500/₹1,000 subsequently demonetised in 2016.
- **MG New Series, 2016 onward:** smaller, distinctive colours; motifs reflect India's heritage/scientific achievements. ₹2,000 was announced in November 2016 with **Mangalyaan**; withdrawal from circulation began in 2023.
- **Reverse motifs:** ₹10—Konark Sun Temple; ₹20—Ellora Caves; ₹50—Hampi with chariot; ₹100—Rani ki Vav; ₹200—Sanchi Stupa; ₹500—Red Fort; ₹2,000—Mangalyaan.

## 12. Cryptocurrency: opportunities and risks

- **Cryptoassets:** cryptographically secured digital assets, often transferred on distributed ledgers. Examples: Bitcoin, Ether (Ethereum network), Litecoin and XRP (associated with Ripple). Decentralisation varies; not all digital money is cryptocurrency.
- **Potential uses:** programmable transfers, some cross-border payments, tokenisation, technology/startup opportunities and financial access. Low cost, inclusion and greater safety are **possible benefits, not guarantees**; internet access, fees, skills and safeguards matter.
- **Risks:** volatility/speculation, exchange/wallet hacks, fraud, consumer losses, illicit finance and monetary/financial-stability challenges. Public chains are often **pseudonymous, not fully anonymous**; transaction tracing is possible.
- Most unbacked crypto has no issuer-guaranteed redemption; lack of gold backing alone is not the decisive difference from fiat money. Stablecoins may have reserves but involve reserve/issuer risk.
- **Environmental cost:** proof-of-work mining can be energy-intensive; not all networks use mining or the same energy model. Crypto does not inherently improve monetary/fiscal-policy control; currency substitution may weaken sovereignty.
- **Indian society:** youth participation and innovation coexist with scams, speculative losses, unequal digital access and regulatory/compliance challenges. Assess financial inclusion against actual usability and consumer protection, rather than assuming universal access.

## 13. India: correct the regulatory timeline

- **April 2018:** RBI restricted regulated entities from providing services connected with virtual currencies; this was not a parliamentary blanket criminal ban on owning/trading crypto.
- **4 March 2020:** Supreme Court set aside that RBI circular in *Internet and Mobile Association of India v. RBI*. The chapter's “May 2020” date is incorrect. In **May 2021**, RBI clarified banks could not rely on the quashed circular; due diligence obligations continued. [RBI clarification](https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_CircularIndexDisplay.aspx?Id=12103)
- **2021 proposed bill:** historical proposal, not an enacted law merely because it was announced. Avoid memorising a proposed blanket ban as existing law.
- **March 2023 onward:** specified VDA service activities fall under **PMLA**; service providers must meet **FIU-IND registration, reporting and AML/CFT obligations**. Thus “crypto has no regulation” is inaccurate. Regulation does not confer legal-tender status. [FIU-IND framework](https://fiuindia.gov.in/pdfs/downloads/VDASP04072023.pdf)
- **Digital rupee (e₹):** RBI-issued CBDC, legal tender and RBI liability. A bank deposit is the bank's liability; **UPI is a payment mechanism**, not a separate currency. Private crypto is distinct from e₹. [RBI digital-rupee FAQ](https://www.rbi.org.in/commonman/Upload/English/FAQs/PDFs/DigitalRupee09012025.pdf)
- **International examples are historical:** El Salvador adopted Bitcoin in **2021**; its **2025 reforms made private acceptance voluntary**. CAR adopted crypto legal-tender provisions in **2022** and revised them in **2023**. Do not use the chapter's two-country list as a current rule. [IMF: El Salvador](https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/cr/2025/english/1slvea2025001-print-pdf.pdf), [IMF: CAR](https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/002/2023/156/article-A001-en.xml)

![Identify the issuer, liability and payment mechanism separately.](Revision%20Diagrams/digital.svg)

*Identify the issuer, liability and payment mechanism separately.*

## 14. Blockchain, NFTs and stablecoins

- **Blockchain:** ledger whose records are grouped into cryptographically linked blocks; participants use consensus to agree on updates. It can be public/permissionless or private/permissioned. Blockchain and cryptocurrency are not synonyms.
- **Tamper resistance:** changing old records is difficult under the system's assumptions, not impossible under every attack/governance arrangement. Security does not automatically protect wallets, exchanges or erroneous inputs.
- **Uses beyond crypto:** supply-chain records, provenance, identity/credential verification and shared registries. Permissionless applications can be built without a central gatekeeper; this does not mean every blockchain has unrestricted access.
- **NFT:** non-fungible token—unique identifier/record; not mutually interchangeable like equal-denomination rupees or units of the same fungible token. Used with artwork, music, collectibles and other assets; can be bought/sold.
- **NFT ownership ≠ automatic copyright or ownership of the underlying work.** Rights depend on the contract/law; links/files can remain off-chain. Fractional arrangements exist, so “never divisible in any form” is too absolute.
- **Stablecoin:** token designed to track a reference value, often a fiat currency. It may use reserves or other mechanisms; **a peg can fail**. It is not automatically government-guaranteed money or a CBDC.

## 15. PYQ recall and quick revision

- **2021 money multiplier:** banking habit increases → currency leakage tends to fall → multiplier rises. **Answer (c).**
- **2020 blockchain:** public-ledger/permissionless descriptions fit the question; crypto-only claim is false. **Statements 1 and 3; answer (d).** Real-world permissioned chains also exist.
- **2013 money demand:** supply unchanged + demand rises → interest rate rises. **Answer (b).**
- **Four functions:** exchange, account, store, deferred payment. **Three motives:** transactions, precautionary, speculative.
- **M₀ uses currency in circulation; M₁ uses currency with public. M₁ includes OD; M₃ adds time deposits.**
- **Multiplier = M₃/M₀; velocity = nominal GDP/M.** Higher banking habit generally raises the former; faster spending raises the latter.
- **Fiat ≠ gold-redeemable; cheque ≠ legal tender; e₹ ≠ UPI; NFT ≠ copyright; stablecoin ≠ guaranteed stability.**
- **Mains answer structure:** define money/technology → explain mechanism → benefits → risks/distributional effects → regulation, literacy, cybersecurity and consumer safeguards. No mains PYQs appear in the supplied chapter; these are answer cues, not PYQs.

1. Money: meaning, functions and qualities

  • Money: anything generally accepted as payment for goods/services and settlement of debts. Legal recognition is important for currency, but all money is not legal tender: bank deposits also function as money.
  • Medium of exchange: removes barter's double coincidence of wants; sell wheat for money, then buy rice.
  • Unit of account: common measure for prices, accounting and comparison.
  • Store of value: transfers purchasing power across time; inflation erodes its real value. Keynes emphasised holding money as an asset; avoid the absolute claim that earlier economists never recognised this function.
  • Standard of deferred payment: denominates future obligations, enabling credit and contracts.
  • Six desirable qualities: acceptability, portability, durability, divisibility, uniformity and controlled scarcity. A payment card is a means of accessing money, not a separate currency.

2. Types of money: distinguish the basis

  • Commodity money: a commodity itself used as money, e.g. gold. Metallic money: coins made of metals. Paper money: notes; these describe material, not necessarily backing.
  • Full-bodied money: commodity/intrinsic value approximately equals face value. Token money: intrinsic value below face value.
  • Representative money: redeemable claim on a backing commodity; representative full-bodied money has equivalent bullion backing held by the issuer. Modern Indian notes are not promises to deliver gold.
  • Fiat money: value rests on legal authority, public confidence and acceptance, without commodity convertibility. “Non-commodity-backed” and “government-backed” describe its features, not two separate types. Market purchasing power is not fixed by government decree alone.
  • Fiduciary/optional money: accepted on trust/agreement, e.g. cheques or bills of exchange; a creditor need not accept these as legal tender. A cheque instructs a deposit transfer; it is not an additional stock of money.
  • Commercial-bank money: deposit balances usable for payment, created partly through lending. Actual money: general textbook label for money used in exchange. Standard money: recognised currency/unit of account; do not confuse this with the intrinsic-value test for full-bodied money.
  • Near money: liquid assets readily convertible into transaction money, e.g. treasury bills, certificates of deposit and short-term deposits. Classification depends on the aggregate: savings-bank deposits may already count as money; they are not universally “outside money”.

13. India: correct the regulatory timeline

  • April 2018: RBI restricted regulated entities from providing services connected with virtual currencies; this was not a parliamentary blanket criminal ban on owning/trading crypto.
  • 4 March 2020: Supreme Court set aside that RBI circular in *Internet and Mobile Association of India v. RBI*. The chapter's “May 2020” date is incorrect. In May 2021, RBI clarified banks could not rely on the quashed circular; due diligence obligations continued. RBI clarification
  • 2021 proposed bill: historical proposal, not an enacted law merely because it was announced. Avoid memorising a proposed blanket ban as existing law.
  • March 2023 onward: specified VDA service activities fall under PMLA; service providers must meet FIU-IND registration, reporting and AML/CFT obligations. Thus “crypto has no regulation” is inaccurate. Regulation does not confer legal-tender status. FIU-IND framework
  • Digital rupee (e₹): RBI-issued CBDC, legal tender and RBI liability. A bank deposit is the bank's liability; UPI is a payment mechanism, not a separate currency. Private crypto is distinct from e₹. RBI digital-rupee FAQ
  • International examples are historical: El Salvador adopted Bitcoin in 2021; its 2025 reforms made private acceptance voluntary. CAR adopted crypto legal-tender provisions in 2022 and revised them in 2023. Do not use the chapter's two-country list as a current rule. IMF: El Salvador, IMF: CAR

14. Blockchain, NFTs and stablecoins

  • Blockchain: ledger whose records are grouped into cryptographically linked blocks; participants use consensus to agree on updates. It can be public/permissionless or private/permissioned. Blockchain and cryptocurrency are not synonyms.
  • Tamper resistance: changing old records is difficult under the system's assumptions, not impossible under every attack/governance arrangement. Security does not automatically protect wallets, exchanges or erroneous inputs.
  • Uses beyond crypto: supply-chain records, provenance, identity/credential verification and shared registries. Permissionless applications can be built without a central gatekeeper; this does not mean every blockchain has unrestricted access.
  • NFT: non-fungible token—unique identifier/record; not mutually interchangeable like equal-denomination rupees or units of the same fungible token. Used with artwork, music, collectibles and other assets; can be bought/sold.
  • NFT ownership ≠ automatic copyright or ownership of the underlying work. Rights depend on the contract/law; links/files can remain off-chain. Fractional arrangements exist, so “never divisible in any form” is too absolute.
  • Stablecoin: token designed to track a reference value, often a fiat currency. It may use reserves or other mechanisms; a peg can fail. It is not automatically government-guaranteed money or a CBDC.

15. PYQ recall and quick revision

  • 2021 money multiplier: banking habit increases → currency leakage tends to fall → multiplier rises. Answer (c).
  • 2020 blockchain: public-ledger/permissionless descriptions fit the question; crypto-only claim is false. Statements 1 and 3; answer (d). Real-world permissioned chains also exist.
  • 2013 money demand: supply unchanged + demand rises → interest rate rises. Answer (b).
  • Four functions: exchange, account, store, deferred payment. Three motives: transactions, precautionary, speculative.
  • M₀ uses currency in circulation; M₁ uses currency with public. M₁ includes OD; M₃ adds time deposits.
  • Multiplier = M₃/M₀; velocity = nominal GDP/M. Higher banking habit generally raises the former; faster spending raises the latter.
  • Fiat ≠ gold-redeemable; cheque ≠ legal tender; e₹ ≠ UPI; NFT ≠ copyright; stablecoin ≠ guaranteed stability.
  • Mains answer structure: define money/technology → explain mechanism → benefits → risks/distributional effects → regulation, literacy, cybersecurity and consumer safeguards. No mains PYQs appear in the supplied chapter; these are answer cues, not PYQs.
