chapters.markdown:
# Income Inequality

## 1. Meaning and causes

- **Inequality:** uneven distribution of income, wealth, resources, services and opportunities. **Income = flow** over a period; **wealth = stock** of assets net of liabilities at a point in time.
- Income inequality concerns **relative shares**, whereas absolute poverty concerns meeting a minimum standard. Poverty can fall while inequality rises; higher average income does not establish equal distribution.
- Causes: **asset concentration**; unequal access to education, skills, health and finance; urban bias in investment; unequal regional infrastructure; discrimination and gender barriers; informality; capital-intensive production that fails to create sufficient productive jobs.
- High prices can hurt households differently depending on their consumption baskets and income adjustment. Inflation does **not automatically** increase every measure of inequality.

## 2. Measure inequality: Lorenz, Gini and Hoover

| Measure | What to remember | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lorenz curve | X: cumulative population, poorest to richest; Y: cumulative income/wealth share | 45-degree line = equality; a curve farther below it generally indicates more inequality |
| Gini coefficient | Area between equality line and Lorenz curve / total area below equality line | **0 = equality; 1 = limiting complete inequality**; also reported on a 0-100 scale |
| Hoover / Robin Hood / Schutz index | Largest vertical gap between equality line and Lorenz curve | Share of total income that would need redistribution to achieve equal shares |

![Gini uses an area ratio; Hoover uses the largest vertical gap.](Revision%20Diagrams/lorenz.svg)

*Gini uses an area ratio; Hoover uses the largest vertical gap.*

- Gini named after **Corrado Gini (1912)**. With shares on a 0-1 scale: **G = 1 - 2 × area under Lorenz curve**.
- Example: Gini **0.29 → 0.36** means greater measured inequality on a comparable series. It does not tell us whether poor people's absolute incomes fell.
- **Hoover = ½ Σ |income share of group - population share of group|**. It is a **maximum gap**, not the shaded area used for Gini.
- If the Lorenz curve coincides with the equality line, **Gini = Hoover = 0**. If two Lorenz curves cross, a simple dominance ranking is unavailable; one summary statistic may hide different distributions.
- Always compare the **same variable, population, method and period**: consumption Gini, income Gini and wealth Gini are different. Household surveys can miss the very rich; tax and national-account estimates also need assumptions.

## 3. India's inequality: keep dates and measures separate

| Indicator | Dated figure | Recall cue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Top 1% income share | **22.6%, 2022-23**, World Inequality Lab study | Income concentration |
| Top 1% wealth share | **40.1%, 2022-23**, same study | Wealth is more concentrated |
| Top 10% / bottom 50% wealth | **77% / 4.1%**, undated figures quoted by book | Source/year unspecified; not WIR 2026 |
| Rural / urban monthly per-capita consumption | **₹3,773 / ₹6,459**, HCES 2022-23, without imputation | Consumption gap, not an income ratio |
| Men's / women's labour-income shares | **82% / 18%**, WIR 2022 figures quoted by book | Aggregate shares, not an equal-work wage-gap estimate |

- **Diet affordability ≠ hunger incidence.** SOFI 2023's historical estimate: about **74% in India** could not afford a healthy diet; about **39% globally**. The book's suggestion that the second figure refers to India is misleading. Both relate to **2021 estimates**, not current rates. [FAO SOFI 2023](https://www.fao.org/interactive/state-of-food-security-nutrition/2023/en/)
- **1922-2023 study:** inequality fell after independence until the early 1980s, then rose, accelerating after the early 2000s. Data span differs: income series back to **1922**, wealth to **1961**. Estimated real average income growth: **1.6% annually, 1960-90; 3.6%, 1990-2022**; fastest subperiods **2005-10: 4.3%; 2010-15: 4.9%**. Income-tax filers rose from under **1% of adults** up to the 1990s to around **5%**, then **9%** in the recent period. Billionaires rose from **1 in 1991 → 52 in 2011 → 162 in 2022**. Top 1% wealth share: **13% in 1961 → about 39% in 2023**. Estimates depend on coverage and reconstruction. [World Inequality Lab working paper](https://wid.world/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/WorldInequalityLab_WP2024_09_Income-and-Wealth-Inequality-in-India-1922-2023_Final.pdf)
- The book's cross-country chart gives **top 1% / top 10% wealth shares**, historical comparison: UK **21.1 / 57.0**; France **24.0 / 57.7**; China **32.6 / 68.8**; India **40.1 / 65.0**; US **34.9 / 70.7**; Brazil **48.7 / 79.7**; South Africa **54.6 / 85.6**. Its common reference year is unspecified; use the pattern, not a current ranking. India's chart shares and the older **77%** figure are from different series/editions.

## 4. World Inequality Report 2026

- Produced by the **World Inequality Lab**, using the World Inequality Database. Distributional estimates combine multiple sources; they are not simply India's consumption-survey results.

| Group in India | Income share | Wealth share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bottom 50% | **15.0%** | **6.4%** |
| Middle 40% | **27.3%** | **28.6%** |
| Top 10% | **57.7%** | **65.0%** |
| Top 1% | **22.6%** | **40.1%** |

- **Top 1% is included within top 10%**: do not add the two shares. The report's country table uses **2024** for this distribution snapshot. [WIR 2026 country tables](https://wir2026.wid.world/www-site/uploads/2026/01/World_Inequality_Report_2026.pdf)
- Global picture highlighted in the book: top 10% receive **over half of income**, bottom half **under 10%**; top 10% own about **three-quarters of wealth**, bottom half about **2%**; top **0.001%** own more wealth than the bottom half combined.
- Climate inequality: top 10% associated with around **77% of private capital ownership emissions**, bottom half about **3%**. This is **not the same accounting as household consumption emissions**. [WIR emissions accounting](https://wir2026.wid.world/insight/executive-summary/)
- Women receive about **28% of global labour income**; roughly **16% in Middle East/North Africa**, around **40% in Europe/North America**. Rich regions' average incomes are around **13 times** those of sub-Saharan Africa in the cited comparison. International finance can favour low-cost borrowing by rich economies while developing economies face higher financing costs. [WIR 2026](https://wid.world/document/world-inequality-report-2026/)

## 5. Reduce inequality: three linked routes

![Combine taxation, services and productive work.](Revision%20Diagrams/policy.svg)

*Combine taxation, services and productive work.*

- **Progressive taxation:** improve effective taxation of high incomes, capital and wealth; close evasion and avoidance channels. A billionaire wealth levy is a **policy proposal**, not an enacted Indian tax. Consider valuation, enforcement, capital mobility and revenue use.
- **Public services and social protection:** education, healthcare, nutrition, infrastructure and income security improve capabilities and reduce unequal starting conditions. Spending quality and access matter as much as totals.
- **Productive jobs:** help workers move from low-productivity agriculture to manufacturing and services; expand labour-intensive industries, MSMEs, skills, credit, women's employment and regional opportunities. Sectoral movement alone is insufficient if new jobs remain precarious.
- **Mains sequence:** distinguish poverty/income/wealth → identify asset and opportunity gaps → give a dated indicator → combine better jobs, services and fair taxation → evaluate inclusion and implementation.
- **Recall:** Lorenz = distribution curve; Gini = area ratio; Hoover = maximum gap; income ≠ wealth ≠ consumption; top 1% is a subset of top 10%.

Editable notesPDF
Browse sections
  1. 1. Meaning and causes
  2. 2. Measure inequality: Lorenz, Gini and Hoover
  3. 3. India's inequality: keep dates and measures separate
  4. 4. World Inequality Report 2026
  5. 5. Reduce inequality: three linked routes

1. Meaning and causes

  • Inequality: uneven distribution of income, wealth, resources, services and opportunities. Income = flow over a period; wealth = stock of assets net of liabilities at a point in time.
  • Income inequality concerns relative shares, whereas absolute poverty concerns meeting a minimum standard. Poverty can fall while inequality rises; higher average income does not establish equal distribution.
  • Causes: asset concentration; unequal access to education, skills, health and finance; urban bias in investment; unequal regional infrastructure; discrimination and gender barriers; informality; capital-intensive production that fails to create sufficient productive jobs.
  • High prices can hurt households differently depending on their consumption baskets and income adjustment. Inflation does not automatically increase every measure of inequality.

2. Measure inequality: Lorenz, Gini and Hoover

MeasureWhat to rememberInterpretation
Lorenz curveX: cumulative population, poorest to richest; Y: cumulative income/wealth share45-degree line = equality; a curve farther below it generally indicates more inequality
Gini coefficientArea between equality line and Lorenz curve / total area below equality line0 = equality; 1 = limiting complete inequality; also reported on a 0-100 scale
Hoover / Robin Hood / Schutz indexLargest vertical gap between equality line and Lorenz curveShare of total income that would need redistribution to achieve equal shares
  • Gini named after Corrado Gini (1912). With shares on a 0-1 scale: G = 1 - 2 × area under Lorenz curve.
  • Example: Gini 0.29 → 0.36 means greater measured inequality on a comparable series. It does not tell us whether poor people's absolute incomes fell.
  • Hoover = ½ Σ |income share of group - population share of group|. It is a maximum gap, not the shaded area used for Gini.
  • If the Lorenz curve coincides with the equality line, Gini = Hoover = 0. If two Lorenz curves cross, a simple dominance ranking is unavailable; one summary statistic may hide different distributions.
  • Always compare the same variable, population, method and period: consumption Gini, income Gini and wealth Gini are different. Household surveys can miss the very rich; tax and national-account estimates also need assumptions.

3. India's inequality: keep dates and measures separate

IndicatorDated figureRecall cue
Top 1% income share22.6%, 2022-23, World Inequality Lab studyIncome concentration
Top 1% wealth share40.1%, 2022-23, same studyWealth is more concentrated

Rural / urban monthly per-capita consumption₹3,773 / ₹6,459, HCES 2022-23, without imputationConsumption gap, not an income ratio
Men's / women's labour-income shares82% / 18%, WIR 2022 figures quoted by bookAggregate shares, not an equal-work wage-gap estimate
  • Diet affordability ≠ hunger incidence. SOFI 2023's historical estimate: about 74% in India could not afford a healthy diet; about 39% globally. The book's suggestion that the second figure refers to India is misleading. Both relate to 2021 estimates, not current rates. FAO SOFI 2023
  • 1922-2023 study: inequality fell after independence until the early 1980s, then rose, accelerating after the early 2000s. Data span differs: income series back to 1922, wealth to 1961. Estimated real average income growth: 1.6% annually, 1960-90; 3.6%, 1990-2022; fastest subperiods 2005-10: 4.3%; 2010-15: 4.9%. Income-tax filers rose from under 1% of adults up to the 1990s to around 5%, then 9% in the recent period. Billionaires rose from 1 in 1991 → 52 in 2011 → 162 in 2022. Top 1% wealth share: 13% in 1961 → about 39% in 2023. Estimates depend on coverage and reconstruction. World Inequality Lab working paper

# Unemployment and Labour Reforms

## 1. Labour force, workforce and core indicators

- **Employed:** doing economic work under the survey's reference-period criteria. **Unemployed:** without employment and seeking or available for work under the applicable survey definition. **Labour force = employed + unemployed**; **workforce = employed only**.
- People outside the labour force include those neither working nor seeking/available for work, such as some students and persons occupied exclusively in domestic duties. Unpaid work in a family enterprise can count as employment; unpaid domestic services are a different category. Statistical employment is about economic activity, not the occupation's legality or whether cash wages are received.
- The book's **15-60** working-age boundary is not universal: the main PLFS figures below cover **age 15 and above**, without an upper limit. Unemployment may be temporary **or persistent**.
- **Labour supply:** hours/person-days offered at a wage; can change without changing the number of workers. **Labour force:** people participating; **workforce:** people employed. The assertion that labour force is unrelated to wages is too strong: wages can affect participation.

| Indicator | Formula | Denominator trap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unemployment rate (UR) | Unemployed / labour force × 100 | Not total population |
| Labour force participation rate (LFPR) | Labour force / relevant population × 100 | Same age group and survey status |
| Worker population ratio (WPR) | Employed / relevant population × 100 | Employment participation |
| Proportion unemployed | Unemployed / relevant population × 100 | Different from UR |
| Employment intensity | Workers / real GDP | Not employment elasticity |
| Employment elasticity | % change in employment / % change in real output | A ratio, not a percentage |

![LFPR and WPR use population; UR uses labour force.](Revision%20Diagrams/classification.svg)

*LFPR and WPR use population; UR uses labour force.*

- Identity: **WPR = LFPR × (1 - UR/100)**. If population = 1,000, labour force = 600 and employed = 570: **LFPR 60%; WPR 57%; UR 5%**; unemployed/population = **3%**.
- A low UR can coexist with low LFPR, disguised unemployment, low earnings or poor-quality work. Discouraged workers leaving the labour force can lower measured unemployment without improving job access.
- Causes in India: insufficient productive jobs; skill/job mismatch; regional and social barriers; demographic pressure; weak education/training links; slow structural transformation and uneven policy implementation.

## 2. Measuring unemployment: reference periods

| Approach | Reference / rule | Best use and limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Usual principal status (UPS / ps) | **365 days**; major-time activity determines principal status | Longer-term attachment; can miss intermittent unemployment |
| Usual status (ps+ss), also called UPSS | Principal status plus subsidiary economic work of **30 days or more** during preceding 365 days | Broader employment identification than UPS |
| Current weekly status (CWS) | **Last 7 days**; at least **1 hour of work on any day** identifies employment | Captures shorter-term changes; intermittent workers can still count as employed |
| Current daily status (CDS), historical EUS method | Daily activity over **7 days**, expressed in person-days | Captures unemployment within a week and underemployment |

- CDS historical rule: **4+ hours of work = full employed day**; **1 to under 4 hours = half employed day**. The remaining half is unemployed only if seeking/available for work; otherwise outside labour force. No work does **not automatically** mean unemployment.
- The **Dantwala Committee (1970)** recommended the activity-status framework; NSS employment surveys used it from **1972-73**. UPS tends to give a lower and CDS a higher estimate because of reference periods and units; this is not an unconditional mathematical ranking for every sample.
- **PLFS began in 2017**, replacing earlier large NSS employment-unemployment rounds; Labour Bureau also ran a separate EUS series. Do not treat all earlier EUS reports as one identical programme.
- First PLFS annual period: **July 2017-June 2018**; education-based stratification and computer-assisted personal interviewing (**CAPI**) improved data collection.
- **From January 2025:** redesigned PLFS provides monthly all-India rural/urban **CWS** indicators, quarterly rural **and** urban CWS estimates, and annual usual-status/CWS estimates. Annual period changed to **January-December**. Design changes limit strict comparability with earlier estimates. [MoSPI PLFS redesign](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2246009&lang=2&reg=48)

## 3. Labour underutilisation and the jobs gap

- **Time-related underemployment:** employed people working insufficient hours who want and are available for more work. They remain employed in the headline UR.
- **Potential labour force:** non-employed persons who either seek work but are not currently available, or are available but have not recently sought work. **Willing non-job seekers:** want work but neither actively seek nor are immediately available.
- **ILO jobs gap** includes unemployed people and other non-employed people who want employment. It captures unmet need beyond the UR.
- Wanting a job is broader than fulfilling availability/search conditions for unemployment. National PLFS formulations and strict international classifications should not be assumed identical in every detail.
- The unemployed component is generally more sensitive to the business cycle; the other components can reflect persistent constraints such as care duties and barriers to participation. The unemployment-inflation relationship is often discussed through the **Phillips curve**, but is not a fixed causal law for the entire jobs gap.

![The jobs gap includes unmet demand beyond the unemployed.](Revision%20Diagrams/gap.svg)

*The jobs gap includes unmet demand beyond the unemployed.*

## 4. Types of unemployment and vulnerable employment

| Type | Defining feature | Example / distinction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Voluntary non-participation | Chooses not to work or seek/accept available work | Usually outside labour force; not automatically counted as unemployment |
| Structural | Jobs and skills/locations do not match; economic structure changes | Reskilling, mobility and job creation needed |
| Disguised | Workers exceed productive requirement; removal need not reduce output | **Marginal product of surplus labour ≈ 0**; common in family agriculture, also elsewhere |
| Frictional | Temporary job-search or matching delay | New entrants and job switchers; layoffs/strikes are not always frictional |
| Cyclical | Aggregate demand falls in a downturn | Recession-related job loss; can occur in any economy |
| Chronic | Persistent unemployment over a long period | Weak investment, skills and employment capacity |
| Technological | Tasks displaced by new production technology | Mechanisation/automation; overlaps structural unemployment |
| Casual | Intermittent absence of work for workers hired day-to-day | Construction or handling work; daily hiring itself is not unemployment |
| Seasonal | Work concentrated in specific seasons | Agriculture or tourism outside peak periods |

- **Vulnerable employment**, not “vulnerable unemployment”: **own-account workers + contributing family workers**. They are employed but often face weak security, low earnings and limited formal protection. Not every self-employed person is vulnerable: employers are a separate category.
- Disguised unemployment reflects low or zero **marginal**, not necessarily zero **average**, productivity. Seasonal unemployment concerns missing work over time, rather than surplus workers at the same task.

## 5. PLFS figures: attach age, period and status

All figures below: **persons aged 15+**. LFPR, WPR and UR are percentages.

| Annual July-June period | Usual LFPR / WPR / UR, all India | CWS LFPR / WPR / UR, all India |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2021-22 | **55.2 / 52.9 / 4.1** | **51.7 / 48.3 / 6.6** |
| 2022-23 | **57.9 / 56.0 / 3.2** | **54.6 / 51.8 / 5.1** |
| 2023-24 | **60.1 / 58.2 / 3.2** | **56.4 / 53.7 / 4.9** |

| Area, 2023-24 | Usual LFPR / WPR / UR | CWS LFPR / WPR / UR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rural | **63.7 / 62.1 / 2.5** | **58.9 / 56.5 / 4.2** |
| Urban | **52.0 / 49.4 / 5.1** | **50.8 / 47.4 / 6.7** |

| Gender, 2023-24 | Usual LFPR / WPR / UR | CWS LFPR / WPR / UR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Male | **78.8 / 76.3 / 3.2** | **77.5 / 73.8 / 4.8** |
| Female | **41.7 / 40.3 / 3.2** | **35.6 / 33.8 / 5.0** |

- **2017-18 → 2023-24, usual:** rural LFPR **50.7 → 63.7**, WPR **48.1 → 62.1**, UR **5.3 → 2.5**; urban LFPR **47.6 → 52.0**, WPR **43.9 → 49.4**, UR **7.7 → 5.1**. Male LFPR/WPR/UR **75.8/71.2/6.1 → 78.8/76.3/3.2**; female **23.3/22.0/5.6 → 41.7/40.3/3.2**.
- **2017-18 → 2023-24, CWS:** rural **48.9/44.8/8.4 → 58.9/56.5/4.2**; urban **47.1/42.6/9.5 → 50.8/47.4/6.7**; male **75.1/68.6/8.7 → 77.5/73.8/4.8**; female **21.1/19.2/9.0 → 35.6/33.8/5.0**.
- Book's older **Labour Bureau 2016-17 UPS** figures: rural **5.2%**, urban **6.1%**, overall **5.4%**; male **4.2%**, female **9.2%**. The book's prose says rural UR is higher, contradicting its own table. Other old claims: LFPR **51.2%**, WPR **47.8%**, about **75% male**, **70% rural** workforce; female worker share about **30% rural / 20% urban**. These figures are not a current PLFS snapshot and lack a consistent denominator in the extract.
- **CMIE June 2024:** book reports overall UR **9.2%**, urban **8.9%**, rural **9.3%**. CMIE is a private Mumbai-based data provider; its methods and monthly estimates differ from PLFS. Do not interpret the gap as a direct contradiction.

### Calendar-year PLFS 2025 update

- Usual-status age 15+: **LFPR 59.3%; WPR 57.4%; UR 3.1%**. Male/female LFPR **79.1/40.0%**, WPR **76.6/38.8%**; UR **3.1%** for both.
- Youth age 15-29 UR **9.9%**; secondary-and-above educated age 15+ UR **6.5%**. Employment status: self-employed **56.2%**, regular wage/salaried **23.6%**, casual **20.2%**. Agriculture accounts for **43.0%** of employment; manufacturing **12.1%**.
- This is a **calendar-year, redesigned survey**. Do not mechanically compare it with July-June 2023-24 as a continuous unchanged series. [PLFS 2025 official release](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2246009&lang=1&reg=1)

## 6. Institutions and data sources

| Institution / headquarters | Function to recall |
| --- | --- |
| Labour Bureau / Chandigarh | Labour statistics; CPI-IW, CPI-AL/RL, wages, industrial disputes, closures, retrenchment and layoffs; labour intelligence, research and evaluation |
| DGFASLI / Mumbai | Directorate General Factory Advice Service and Labour Institutes; established **1945**; factory safety advice, training and coordination |
| DGMS / Dhanbad | Directorate General of Mines Safety; mine occupational safety and health |
| DTNBWED / New Delhi | Dattopant Thengadi National Board for Workers Education and Development; established **1958**; workers' education across organised, unorganised and rural sectors; earlier headquartered in Nagpur |
| V.V. Giri National Labour Institute / Noida | Autonomous labour research, training, education and consultancy body; **1974** |
| Indian Labour Archives / Noida | At VVGNLI; **1998**, preservation/access to working-class historical records |

| Survey / report | Producer and coverage | Limitation / use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PLFS | NSO, MoSPI; household employment and unemployment | Reference period and age must match |
| Earlier EUS | NSS employment surveys and separate Labour Bureau series | Distinguish their samples and years |
| QES | Labour Bureau; establishments with **10+ workers**, nine selected non-farm sectors | Not all employment in India |
| ASUSE | NSO, MoSPI; unincorporated non-agricultural manufacturing, trade and other services, excluding construction | Establishment characteristics and employment |
| Payroll reporting | MoSPI; EPFO, ESIC and NPS administrative subscriptions | Enrolment/formalisation ≠ unique net new jobs; avoid double-counting across schemes |
| Occupational Wage Survey | Labour Bureau; selected services, plantations, mines and manufacturing | Occupational wage data; WRI weights |
| Wage Rate Index | Labour Bureau; **2016 = 100**, 37 selected industries in book | Wage-rate change; not CPI or number of jobs |
| Other Labour Bureau reports | Worker conditions including SC/ST, unorganised industries, minimum-wage evaluation; disputes, absenteeism, closures, retrenchment, layoffs | Institutional association is a PYQ cue |

- **QES January-March 2022:** estimated **3.18 crore**, rounded **3.2 crore** workers; manufacturing largest contributor; **86.4% regular**, **1.9% self-employed**; women **31.8%**, men **68.2%**. Nine sectors: manufacturing, construction, trade, transport, education, health, accommodation/restaurants, IT/BPO and financial services. The **83%** benchmark refers to employment in these sectors among establishments with 10+ workers in the **2013-14 Economic Census**, not 83% of India's entire workforce. [Official QES release](https://labour.gov.in/sites/default/files/pib1862597.pdf)
- EPFO net payroll additions quoted by book: **61.1 lakh FY2018-19 → 131.5 lakh FY2023-24**. Includes both employment and formalisation effects; registrations alone cannot prove job creation.
- **ILO WESO Trends 2025:** global UR **5.0% in 2024** versus **5.1% in 2023**. Book quotes high-/low-income-country UR **4.5/5.7%** and men's jobs-gap rates **7.1/15.2%**. Keep report year, estimate year, gender and country grouping; an unemployment rate and jobs-gap rate have different scopes. [ILO WESO 2025](https://www.ilo.org/publications/flagship-reports/world-employment-and-social-outlook-trends-2025)

- DTNBWED head-office location: [official RTI manual](https://dtnbwed.cbwe.gov.in/images/upload/RTI-Manual---DTNBWED-2022_9DRL.pdf).

## 7. Occupational structure and time use

| Workforce, book's 2023-24 classification | Primary | Secondary | Tertiary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All India | **44.5%** | **25.6%** | **29.9%** |
| Rural | **57.3%** | **22.8%** | **19.9%** |
| Urban | **5.8%** | **31.5%** | **62.7%** |

- Rural work concentrated in primary activities; urban work in services. Book's long-run comparison: **1950-51 = 72.7/10.0/17.3%**; later rounded **45/25/30%**, labelled 2024-25 without a clear source. Use the trend of structural change; do not substitute the rounded row for an official PLFS year.
- **Time Use Survey (TUS): NSO/MoSPI**, second all-India round **2024**, first **2019**. Measures participation and duration in paid and unpaid activities over a **24-hour** reference day.
- Age 15-59 in employment/related activities: rounded male/female participation **75/25% in 2024**, versus **70.9/21.8% in 2019**. Female participants in unpaid domestic services spent **305 minutes/day in 2024**, down from **315 in 2019**. Caregiving participation: women **41%**, men **21.4%**. These are activity participation/time-use measures, not PLFS LFPR. [TUS 2024 release](https://www.pib.gov.in/Pressreleaseshare.aspx?PRID=2106113&lang=2&reg=48)
- Care burdens constrain paid work. Childcare, safe transport, flexible decent work and shared domestic responsibility can improve women's participation. A fall in unpaid minutes alone does not establish why paid work changed.

## 8. Jobless growth, employment elasticity and Beveridge curve

- **Jobless growth:** output expands with little or inadequate employment expansion. Merely having output growth faster than employment growth does not, by itself, prove no jobs were created; productivity gains normally create such a difference.
- Drivers: labour-saving technology; skill-intensive growth; insufficient labour-intensive manufacturing; weak MSME credit/infrastructure; skill mismatch; disguised employment; poor implementation of labour reforms.
- Services are heterogeneous: IT can be skill-intensive, while tourism, retail and care can absorb much labour. **FDI is not inherently job-destroying**; its net effect depends on sector, technology, linkages and investment. The book's assertion that capital shortage forces labour-saving technology is not a general economic rule.
- Historical elasticity estimates quoted: **0.52 (1972-73 to 1983)** → **0.41 (next decade)** → **0.29 (1993-94 to 2004-05)** → **0.04 (2004-05 to 2011-12)**; agriculture **0.46 → -0.42** across cited first/last periods. These are **dimensionless ratios**, not 0.52% etc.; negative elasticity can mean labour exits a growing sector. The book's 1951-2000 GDP/employment-growth comparisons are broad historical claims, not a current forecast.
- **Beveridge / UV curve:** X = unemployment rate; Y = vacancy rate; usually slopes downward. Recession: move toward **high unemployment, low vacancies**; expansion: reverse. **Outward shift** suggests weaker matching, mismatch or other structural frictions; not merely a cyclical movement.

![Recession moves along the curve; matching problems can shift it outward.](Revision%20Diagrams/beveridge.svg)

*Recession moves along the curve; matching problems can shift it outward.*

## 9. Casualisation and informal employment

- NSO employment-status groups: **self-employed**, **regular wage/salaried**, **casual labour**. Self-employed includes employers, own-account workers and unpaid helpers in household enterprises.
- **Casualisation:** greater reliance on day-to-day or short-duration hiring. Drivers include rural-to-urban migration without suitable skills, construction expansion and employers' flexible hiring practices.
- **Informal sector ≠ informal employment.** Enterprise classification depends on ownership/size/registration; employment classification concerns social protection, contract and benefits. **Informal jobs exist inside organised/formal enterprises**; regular salary does not guarantee formal protection. The book's simple 10-worker cutoff cannot establish whether every worker is formal.
- Casual workers can be legally eligible for EPF and wage/hour protections when coverage conditions apply. Permanent status does not automatically guarantee actual compliance; not every casual worker receives every benefit.
- Book's **“90% informal / 10% formal”** is a broad, undated approximation, not a current measured split. Migration, skills gaps, firm size, compliance costs, contracting and weak enforcement can increase vulnerability; market reforms alone do not demonstrate a single causal explanation.
- Responses: quality vocational education; apprenticeships; credit and infrastructure for productive self-employment; MSME growth; simpler compliance with effective enforcement; portable social security and migrant-worker support. Self-employment without income/security improvement is not an automatic cure.

## 10. Employment and skill initiatives

| Scheme / institution | Recall purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Atmanirbhar Bharat Rojgar Yojana (ABRY) | COVID-era employment/formalisation incentive in Atmanirbhar Bharat 3.0; time-bound, not a permanent universal subsidy |
| EDLI | Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance; death-in-service insurance for eligible EPF members' beneficiaries, not unemployment allowance |
| SMILE / Social Justice Ministry | Support for Marginalised Individuals for Livelihood and Enterprise; umbrella rehabilitation including persons engaged in begging and transgender persons |
| PM-DAKSH / Social Justice Ministry | Pradhan Mantri Dakshta Aur Kushalta Sampann Hitgrahi; skill training for targeted disadvantaged groups through portal/app |
| PMKVY 4.0 / Skill Development Ministry | Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana; employable skills, including emerging technologies; book mentions 300+ courses |
| PMEGP / MSME Ministry, KVIC | Credit-linked subsidy to establish non-farm micro-enterprises and support self-employment |
| FutureSkills PRIME / MeitY-NASSCOM | Reskilling/upskilling in emerging digital technologies including AI |
| DDU-GKY / Rural Development Ministry | Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana; placement-linked skills for poor rural youth, with inclusion provisions; not exclusively SC/ST/minority/women |
| STRIVE | Skills Strengthening for Industrial Value Enhancement; World Bank-supported project improving ITIs and apprenticeships; retain as project-era initiative |

- MGNREGA provides rural wage employment and public works; its jobs should not be assumed identical to private construction-sector employment. Evaluate initiatives through placements, retention, earnings and additional jobs, not training/enrolment totals alone.

## 11. Labour reform and the four codes

- Labour is mainly in the **Concurrent List**: Union and States legislate. Reform seeks productivity, employment and simpler compliance while protecting wages, safety, collective bargaining and social security; the **Second National Commission on Labour** recommended consolidation.
- **Four codes rationalise 29 central labour laws.** Government made them effective from **21 November 2025**. Distinguish enactment, commencement and specific operational rules/coverage. [Official commencement announcement](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2192463&lang=1&reg=3)

| Code | Laws consolidated | Core provisions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Code on Wages, **2019** | **4** | Minimum wages, timely payment, bonus and gender non-discrimination; Centre fixes floor wage; minimum wages cannot be below the applicable floor |
| Industrial Relations Code, **2020** | **3** | Trade unions/negotiating arrangements, standing orders, disputes, strike/lockout notice, retrenchment/closure permission where applicable, reskilling fund |
| Code on Social Security, **2020** | **9** | EPF/ESI and other social security; enabling schemes for unorganised, gig/platform workers and funding contributions |
| Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, **2020** | **13** | Safety, health, working conditions; **8-hour daily work framework**; contract labour; interstate migrants; women's employment with consent and safeguards |

- **Correction:** book prints Social Security **8 laws** and OSH Code **2019**. Correct recall: **4 + 3 + 9 + 13 = 29; years 2019 + three 2020 codes**. [Social Security Code text](https://labour.gov.in/sites/default/files/ss_code_as_passed_by_lok_sabha.pdf)
- Gig/platform recognition and funds do not mean every worker immediately receives every contributory benefit. Coverage depends on applicable provisions, notified schemes and implementation.
- **Fixed-term employment, 2018 standing-order rules:** extended provision across sectors; written contract for fixed duration; comparable hours, wages, allowances and proportionate statutory benefits; rule barred conversion of existing permanent posts to fixed-term posts. Expiry of agreed term differs from retrenchment before expiry; the book's “no notice” statement is not a general permission to dismiss anyone without process.
- Trade-off: flexibility and simpler hiring versus repeated short contracts, insecurity, bargaining weakness and evasion. Combine enforceable parity/benefits and skills with predictable hiring rules.

## 12. Pension and social-security schemes

| Scheme | Eligibility / contribution | Benefit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PM Shram Yogi Maan-dhan (PM-SYM), **2019** | Unorganised workers **18-40**, monthly income **≤ ₹15,000**; not covered by EPFO/ESIC or government-funded NPS; not income-tax payers; age-linked member contribution matched by Centre | Minimum **₹3,000/month pension from 60** |
| National Pension Scheme for Traders, Shopkeepers and Self-Employed, **2019** | **18-40**, annual turnover **≤ ₹1.5 crore**; exclusions include EPFO/ESIC/NPS/PM-SYM coverage and income-tax payers; member and Centre contribute equally | Minimum **₹3,000/month from 60** |
| Atal Pension Yojana (APY) | Indian citizens **18-40**, bank/post-office savings account; age/pension-linked contributions; **income-tax payers barred from new enrolment from 1 October 2022** | Guaranteed minimum **₹1,000-₹5,000/month from 60**, depending on selected pension/contributions |

- PM-SYM and traders' schemes are under the **Labour Ministry**; APY is under the **Finance Ministry/PFRDA**, not the same scheme. [PM-SYM eligibility](https://www.epfindia.gov.in/site_docs/PDFs/PQ_PDFs/PQ_WinterSession_2023_English.pdf), [APY FAQ](https://www.pfrda.org.in/w/faqs/atal-pension-yojana)
- **EPF:** EPFO under Labour Ministry; covered establishments generally **20+ employees**. Standard employee contribution **12% of applicable wages**; employer contribution generally **12%**, split between EPF and EPS for eligible pension members. Book's **3.67% EPF + 8.33% EPS** is the standard illustrative employer split, subject to EPS eligibility and ceiling; not 12% of every person's entire gross salary.
- Book's EPF mandatory wage ceiling **₹15,000** is historical. Government raised it to **₹25,000/month effective 17 September 2026**. Existing membership normally continues when wages rise above the ceiling; do not say existing members can simply opt out. [Official EPF ceiling revision](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=2310973&lang=2&reg=48)
- **ESI:** ESIC's integrated medical/cash protection for covered workers and dependants against sickness, maternity, employment injury, disablement and death. Book's general insured-wage ceiling **₹21,000/month** is distinct from EPF's ceiling; disability-specific exceptions and establishment coverage matter.
- **EDLI = insurance; EPF = savings; EPS/APY/PM-SYM = pensions; ESI = medical and cash protection.** Eligibility and actual coverage, not job label alone, determine benefits.

## 13. AI and the labour force

![AI exposure and net job losses are different concepts.](Revision%20Diagrams/ai.svg)

*AI exposure and net job losses are different concepts.*

- AI may automate tasks, complement workers, raise productivity and create new occupations. **Task exposure is not observed job loss**; the book's “75 million jobs at complete risk” is a modelled older claim, not a verified tally of jobs eliminated.
- Risks: displacement of routine IT/service tasks; skill polarisation; wage/income inequality; surveillance and bias; weak regulatory capacity; consumption slowdown if livelihoods suffer. Emerging economies can face adoption and adjustment constraints alongside opportunities.
- **ILO's 2025 analysis emphasises job transformation and augmentation**, with outcomes differing by occupation, gender and digital infrastructure. [ILO AI research](https://www.ilo.org/publications/artificial-intelligence-adoption-and-its-impact-jobs)
- Economic Survey **2023-24** estimated a need for roughly **78.5 lakh additional non-farm jobs annually to 2030**; this is a planning requirement, not measured annual creation.
- Response: foundational education; continuous reskilling; affordable digital access; worker consultation; portable social security; safeguards for bias/privacy; support labour-intensive and care/green sectors; strengthen labour-market institutions. Assess net jobs, earnings and job quality, not productivity alone.

## 14. PYQs and answer cues

- **Prelims 2022:** industrial disputes, closures, retrenchment and layoffs → **Labour Bureau (c)**.
- **Prelims 2021:** casual workers' PF coverage, working hours/overtime and notified bank-only wage payment → source key **all three (d)**. Apply legal coverage conditions; “casual” does not itself exclude a worker from protections.
- **Prelims 2013:** disguised unemployment → **marginal productivity of labour is zero (c)**.
- **Mains 2023:** structural unemployment → define mismatch; compare usual/CWS/CDS methods and denominators; explain missing underemployment, discouragement, care and job quality; propose higher-frequency surveys, skill/vacancy mapping, better administrative-data integration and comparable reporting.
- **Mains 2015:** jobless-growth debate → compare employment elasticity, sector mix and job quality; distinguish productivity-led output growth from zero jobs; discuss informality/measurement; propose labour-intensive manufacturing, MSMEs, skills and service opportunities with evidence.
- **Recall:** UR denominator = labour force; WPR = population; usual = 365 days, CWS = 7 days; employed ≠ adequately employed; informal job ≠ informal enterprise; enactment ≠ commencement; elasticity is a ratio.

1. Labour force, workforce and core indicators

  • Employed: doing economic work under the survey's reference-period criteria. Unemployed: without employment and seeking or available for work under the applicable survey definition. Labour force = employed + unemployed; workforce = employed only.
  • People outside the labour force include those neither working nor seeking/available for work, such as some students and persons occupied exclusively in domestic duties. Unpaid work in a family enterprise can count as employment; unpaid domestic services are a different category. Statistical employment is about economic activity, not the occupation's legality or whether cash wages are received.
  • The book's 15-60 working-age boundary is not universal: the main PLFS figures below cover age 15 and above, without an upper limit. Unemployment may be temporary or persistent.
  • Labour supply: hours/person-days offered at a wage; can change without changing the number of workers. Labour force: people participating; workforce: people employed. The assertion that labour force is unrelated to wages is too strong: wages can affect participation.
IndicatorFormulaDenominator trap
Unemployment rate (UR)Unemployed / labour force × 100Not total population
Labour force participation rate (LFPR)Labour force / relevant population × 100Same age group and survey status
Worker population ratio (WPR)Employed / relevant population × 100Employment participation
Proportion unemployedUnemployed / relevant population × 100Different from UR
Employment intensityWorkers / real GDPNot employment elasticity
Employment elasticity% change in employment / % change in real outputA ratio, not a percentage
  • Identity: WPR = LFPR × (1 - UR/100). If population = 1,000, labour force = 600 and employed = 570: LFPR 60%; WPR 57%; UR 5%; unemployed/population = 3%.
  • A low UR can coexist with low LFPR, disguised unemployment, low earnings or poor-quality work. Discouraged workers leaving the labour force can lower measured unemployment without improving job access.
  • Causes in India: insufficient productive jobs; skill/job mismatch; regional and social barriers; demographic pressure; weak education/training links; slow structural transformation and uneven policy implementation.

2. Measuring unemployment: reference periods

ApproachReference / ruleBest use and limitation
Usual principal status (UPS / ps)365 days; major-time activity determines principal statusLonger-term attachment; can miss intermittent unemployment
Usual status (ps+ss), also called UPSSPrincipal status plus subsidiary economic work of 30 days or more during preceding 365 daysBroader employment identification than UPS
Current weekly status (CWS)Last 7 days; at least 1 hour of work on any day identifies employmentCaptures shorter-term changes; intermittent workers can still count as employed
Current daily status (CDS), historical EUS methodDaily activity over 7 days, expressed in person-daysCaptures unemployment within a week and underemployment
  • CDS historical rule: 4+ hours of work = full employed day; 1 to under 4 hours = half employed day. The remaining half is unemployed only if seeking/available for work; otherwise outside labour force. No work does not automatically mean unemployment.
  • The Dantwala Committee (1970) recommended the activity-status framework; NSS employment surveys used it from 1972-73. UPS tends to give a lower and CDS a higher estimate because of reference periods and units; this is not an unconditional mathematical ranking for every sample.
  • PLFS began in 2017, replacing earlier large NSS employment-unemployment rounds; Labour Bureau also ran a separate EUS series. Do not treat all earlier EUS reports as one identical programme.
  • First PLFS annual period: July 2017-June 2018; education-based stratification and computer-assisted personal interviewing (CAPI) improved data collection.
  • From January 2025: redesigned PLFS provides monthly all-India rural/urban CWS indicators, quarterly rural and urban CWS estimates, and annual usual-status/CWS estimates. Annual period changed to January-December. Design changes limit strict comparability with earlier estimates. MoSPI PLFS redesign

3. Labour underutilisation and the jobs gap

  • Time-related underemployment: employed people working insufficient hours who want and are available for more work. They remain employed in the headline UR.
  • Potential labour force: non-employed persons who either seek work but are not currently available, or are available but have not recently sought work. Willing non-job seekers: want work but neither actively seek nor are immediately available.
  • ILO jobs gap includes unemployed people and other non-employed people who want employment. It captures unmet need beyond the UR.
  • Wanting a job is broader than fulfilling availability/search conditions for unemployment. National PLFS formulations and strict international classifications should not be assumed identical in every detail.
  • The unemployed component is generally more sensitive to the business cycle; the other components can reflect persistent constraints such as care duties and barriers to participation. The unemployment-inflation relationship is often discussed through the Phillips curve, but is not a fixed causal law for the entire jobs gap.

4. Types of unemployment and vulnerable employment

TypeDefining featureExample / distinction
Voluntary non-participationChooses not to work or seek/accept available workUsually outside labour force; not automatically counted as unemployment
StructuralJobs and skills/locations do not match; economic structure changesReskilling, mobility and job creation needed
DisguisedWorkers exceed productive requirement; removal need not reduce outputMarginal product of surplus labour ≈ 0; common in family agriculture, also elsewhere
FrictionalTemporary job-search or matching delayNew entrants and job switchers; layoffs/strikes are not always frictional
CyclicalAggregate demand falls in a downturnRecession-related job loss; can occur in any economy
ChronicPersistent unemployment over a long periodWeak investment, skills and employment capacity
TechnologicalTasks displaced by new production technologyMechanisation/automation; overlaps structural unemployment
CasualIntermittent absence of work for workers hired day-to-dayConstruction or handling work; daily hiring itself is not unemployment
SeasonalWork concentrated in specific seasonsAgriculture or tourism outside peak periods
  • Vulnerable employment, not “vulnerable unemployment”: own-account workers + contributing family workers. They are employed but often face weak security, low earnings and limited formal protection. Not every self-employed person is vulnerable: employers are a separate category.
  • Disguised unemployment reflects low or zero marginal, not necessarily zero average, productivity. Seasonal unemployment concerns missing work over time, rather than surplus workers at the same task.

8. Jobless growth, employment elasticity and Beveridge curve

  • Jobless growth: output expands with little or inadequate employment expansion. Merely having output growth faster than employment growth does not, by itself, prove no jobs were created; productivity gains normally create such a difference.
  • Drivers: labour-saving technology; skill-intensive growth; insufficient labour-intensive manufacturing; weak MSME credit/infrastructure; skill mismatch; disguised employment; poor implementation of labour reforms.
  • Services are heterogeneous: IT can be skill-intensive, while tourism, retail and care can absorb much labour. FDI is not inherently job-destroying; its net effect depends on sector, technology, linkages and investment. The book's assertion that capital shortage forces labour-saving technology is not a general economic rule.
  • Historical elasticity estimates quoted: 0.52 (1972-73 to 1983) → 0.41 (next decade) → 0.29 (1993-94 to 2004-05) → 0.04 (2004-05 to 2011-12); agriculture 0.46 → -0.42 across cited first/last periods. These are dimensionless ratios, not 0.52% etc.; negative elasticity can mean labour exits a growing sector. The book's 1951-2000 GDP/employment-growth comparisons are broad historical claims, not a current forecast.
  • Beveridge / UV curve: X = unemployment rate; Y = vacancy rate; usually slopes downward. Recession: move toward high unemployment, low vacancies; expansion: reverse. Outward shift suggests weaker matching, mismatch or other structural frictions; not merely a cyclical movement.

9. Casualisation and informal employment

  • NSO employment-status groups: self-employed, regular wage/salaried, casual labour. Self-employed includes employers, own-account workers and unpaid helpers in household enterprises.
  • Casualisation: greater reliance on day-to-day or short-duration hiring. Drivers include rural-to-urban migration without suitable skills, construction expansion and employers' flexible hiring practices.
  • Informal sector ≠ informal employment. Enterprise classification depends on ownership/size/registration; employment classification concerns social protection, contract and benefits. Informal jobs exist inside organised/formal enterprises; regular salary does not guarantee formal protection. The book's simple 10-worker cutoff cannot establish whether every worker is formal.
  • Casual workers can be legally eligible for EPF and wage/hour protections when coverage conditions apply. Permanent status does not automatically guarantee actual compliance; not every casual worker receives every benefit.
  • Book's “90% informal / 10% formal” is a broad, undated approximation, not a current measured split. Migration, skills gaps, firm size, compliance costs, contracting and weak enforcement can increase vulnerability; market reforms alone do not demonstrate a single causal explanation.
  • Responses: quality vocational education; apprenticeships; credit and infrastructure for productive self-employment; MSME growth; simpler compliance with effective enforcement; portable social security and migrant-worker support. Self-employment without income/security improvement is not an automatic cure.

  • Prelims 2013: disguised unemployment → marginal productivity of labour is zero (c).
  • Mains 2023: structural unemployment → define mismatch; compare usual/CWS/CDS methods and denominators; explain missing underemployment, discouragement, care and job quality; propose higher-frequency surveys, skill/vacancy mapping, better administrative-data integration and comparable reporting.

  • Recall: UR denominator = labour force; WPR = population; usual = 365 days, CWS = 7 days; employed ≠ adequately employed; informal job ≠ informal enterprise; enactment ≠ commencement; elasticity is a ratio.

# Inflation

## Meaning, formula and base effect

**Inflation = sustained rise in the general price level; purchasing power of money falls.** A rise in one commodity alone is a relative-price change, not necessarily general inflation.

**YoY inflation (%) = [(current index / index in the same month last year) - 1] × 100.** Month-on-month inflation uses the preceding month. The **base year** anchors an index at 100; the **comparison base** is the earlier period used to calculate inflation.

**Base effect:** a high comparison-period price level can lower measured inflation even while current prices rise. Example: index 100 → 110 → 115.5 gives inflation 10% → 5%; prices have not fallen.

![Prices rise; inflation can slow](Revision%20Diagrams/base.svg)

Choose a recent, representative base year and revise weights when consumption/production patterns change. Avoid treating an abnormal drought, crisis or price spike as representative. Index levels from differently based series cannot be compared directly.

## Types: do not confuse the terms

| Term | Meaning / memory cue |
|---|---|
| Creeping | Slow inflation; textbook convention around 2-3% annually |
| Walking / trotting | Moderate inflation; textbook range 3-10% annually |
| Galloping | Rapid inflation; the supplied text uses above 10% up to 50% annually |
| Hyperinflation | Conventional Cagan threshold: above **50% per month**, not per year; money loses its store-of-value role |
| Disinflation | Inflation slows, e.g. 8% → 4%; prices still rise |
| Deflation | Sustained fall in the general price level; real debt burden rises |
| Reflation | Policy stimulus to restore demand/output and counter deflation or recession |
| Stagflation | High inflation + weak/stagnant growth + high unemployment |
| Skewflation | Non-standard term for divergent sectoral prices, e.g. food inflation alongside falling prices elsewhere |

These speed bands are descriptive conventions, not RBI statutory categories. Historical hyperinflation examples: Germany in the early 1920s, Hungary in 1946 and Zimbabwe in the 2000s. Reflation may use fiscal spending/tax relief and monetary easing; currency printing is not its sole instrument.

## Why prices rise

| Type | Trigger | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Demand-pull | Aggregate demand outruns available output/capacity | Fiscal stimulus, private spending, credit expansion, exports, higher purchasing power |
| Cost-push | Costs rise or supply contracts | Oil/import prices, currency depreciation, wages beyond productivity, indirect taxes, drought/floods, supply-chain disruption |
| Structural / bottleneck | Persistent supply rigidities prevent response | Low agricultural productivity, poor storage/logistics, fragmented markets, shortages |

**Demand ≠ automatic inflation:** greater demand can initially raise output when spare capacity exists. Wage indexation can sustain a wage-price spiral but is not itself the same as an initial demand shock. Higher interest rates normally restrain demand. Depreciation can support exports and also raise imported input costs.

![Identify the inflation channel](Revision%20Diagrams/causes.svg)

**India:** volatile monsoons/El Niño, perishable-food shortages, oil-import dependence, geopolitical disruption (including Russia-Ukraine), hoarding, distribution costs and changing diets. MSP increases may affect some prices; the effect depends on procurement, supply response and market conditions. Monetised deficits can add inflationary pressure; productive public investment may instead expand capacity over time.

## Price indices: current series and historical series

| Indicator | Measures / compiler | Base and exam distinction |
|---|---|---|
| CPI Rural / Urban / Combined | Household consumption prices of goods **and services**; NSO, MoSPI | **2024=100**, released from January 2026; earlier headline series **2012=100** |
| CPI-IW | Industrial workers; Labour Bureau, Ministry of Labour & Employment | **2016=100**; used for wage/DA indexation |
| CPI-AL / CPI-RL | Agricultural / rural labourers; Labour Bureau | **2019=100**, replacing 1986-87 from June 2025 releases |
| WPI | Goods prices upstream; Office of Economic Adviser, DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce & Industry | **2022-23=100**, launched 15 June 2026; replaces **2011-12=100** |
| GDP deflator | Prices of domestically produced final goods/services in GDP; national accounts | Implicit index: nominal GDP / real GDP × 100 |
| PPI | Producer output prices / input costs, with separate series | Indian output, trial input and seven service PPIs launched in June 2026, base **2022-23** |

### CPI and consumer food prices

- **Headline inflation:** change in the full CPI basket. **Core inflation:** usually excludes food and fuel; the exact exclusion must be stated. Refined core may also exclude petrol, diesel and lubricants within transport.
- CPI reflects consumer living costs and is India's monetary-policy anchor. It includes retail margins and relevant consumer taxes, unlike a basic-price producer index.
- The **2024 series** uses HCES 2023-24 consumption information and COICOP 2018 classification. Food-and-beverages weight is **36.75%**; the old 2012 classification weight was **45.86%**. A like-for-like COICOP reclassification of the old series gives **42.62%**, so the raw change also reflects classification changes.
- **Consumer Food Price Index (CFPI):** a food subset of CPI; not identical to the entire CPI food-and-beverages division. Old claims about 2012 weights and rural housing must be read with that series label; the 2024 series also measures rural housing.
- NSO was formed by integrating CSO and NSSO in 2019. DA for industrial workers is linked to **CPI-IW**, not automatically to CPI Combined.

[CPI methodology and January 2026 release](https://www.mospi.gov.in/uploads/latestreleasesfiles/1770893247472-Press%20Relase%20of%20CPI%20for%20Jan26.pdf); [Labour Bureau index bases](https://stglbchd.labourbureau.gov.in/).

### WPI: retain both series for PYQs

| Feature | 2011-12 series (historical) | 2022-23 series (June 2026 onward) |
|---|---|---|
| Number of goods | 697 | 957 |
| Primary articles weight | 22.62% | 22.76% |
| Fuel and power weight | 13.15% | 14.11% |
| Manufactured products weight | 64.23% | 63.13% |
| Weight derivation | Net traded value | Gross value of output |

The new series adds solar, wind and nuclear electricity; moves crude petroleum/natural gas into fuel and power. **WPI Food Index = food articles + manufactured food products**, not all goods. WPI does not become a services index merely because separate service PPIs now exist. Current WPI is monthly; the 2010 PYQ refers to its older weekly reporting context. The modern quick series began in 1942; earlier historical records also exist.

[2026 WPI/PPI launch](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2272872&lang=1&reg=3); [new WPI base announcement](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2267963&lang=1&reg=20).

### GDP deflator and PPI

**GDP deflator = nominal GDP / real GDP × 100.** If nominal GDP is 220 and real GDP is 200, deflator = 110. This means prices are 10% above the reference level; it does **not** prove current-year inflation is 10%. Deflator inflation requires comparison with the previous period's deflator.

- Includes domestic final consumption, investment, government output and exports; imports are not directly part of domestic production.
- Its composition can change with output; CPI instead represents household consumption. Neither measure is universally 'best'. GDP estimates/deflators are available quarterly and annually, not as a monthly consumer-price measure.
- **PPI:** producer prices received, distinct from consumer prices paid. The B.N. Goldar working group (2014) recommended PPI development; the claim that India has no PPI is now historical.
- New output PPI is monthly; manufacturing input PPI is **experimental**; seven service PPIs are quarterly. Output/service PPI uses basic prices; trial input PPI uses purchasers' prices. Service coverage is selective, not the whole service economy. [DPIIT launch and release arrangements](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2272872&lang=1&reg=3).

### Other indices

**FAO Food Price Index:** international traded food prices; cereals, vegetable oils, dairy, meat and sugar. **January 2026:** 123.9 points, down 0.4% month-on-month; this is a dated global indicator, not India's retail inflation. [FAO January release](https://www.fao.org/countryprofiles/news-archive/detail-news/en/c/1757234/).

**House Price Index:** residential property-price movement. The supplied RBI **2010-11 base, ten-city** description refers to the older series. Do not confuse it with **NHB RESIDEX**, a separate housing index. Property-price inflation need not move with headline CPI.

## Who gains and who loses?

| Group / channel | Effect, subject to conditions |
|---|---|
| Fixed nominal debtors | Unexpected inflation reduces real repayment burden |
| Lenders / fixed-income recipients | Lose purchasing power unless adequately compensated/indexed |
| Existing fixed-rate bonds | Higher market interest rates generally lower market prices |
| Businesses | May gain if selling prices rise faster than costs; squeezed if costs outrun prices |
| Poor households | Food inflation hurts disproportionately; real wages may lag |
| Savers | Negative real returns can encourage gold/property holdings |
| External sector | Higher domestic inflation may erode competitiveness; depreciation has mixed effects |
| Government | Nominal revenues may rise, but subsidies, wages, interest and procurement costs can also rise |

**Inflation tax:** erosion of purchasing power of money balances. **Inflation premium:** component of nominal interest compensating expected inflation. **Real interest ≈ nominal interest - inflation**; exact relation is (1 + nominal)/(1 + inflation) - 1. A bank's loan-deposit spread is not the definition of inflation premium.

Inflation does not inevitably increase employment, reduce saving, depreciate currency or produce stagflation. Outcomes depend on expectations, policy, supply and whether inflation was anticipated.

## Phillips curve and inflation targeting

**A.W. Phillips (1958)** originally examined wage inflation and unemployment. A short-run inverse relationship can occur under given expectations; supply shocks and changing expectations shift the curve. No permanent long-run employment gain follows from ever-higher inflation. The 1970s oil shocks illustrated stagflation and challenged a stable trade-off.

**Urjit Patel committee:** constituted 2013, report 2014; recommended CPI as nominal anchor and a transparent inflation-targeting framework. Monetary Policy Framework Agreement: **2015**; statutory framework in the RBI Act, 1934: **2016**.

**Flexible inflation targeting:** price stability while keeping growth in mind; not a rule to ignore output or employment. Central Government fixes the target in consultation with RBI under **section 45ZA**. Target = **4% CPI inflation**, tolerance **2-6%**. Renewed for **1 April 2026-31 March 2031**, after the 2016-21 and 2021-26 periods. [Gazette notification S.O. 1580(E)](https://gazettetracker.com/g/CG-DL-E-25032026-271285).

**Failure criterion:** average inflation above 6% or below 2% for three consecutive quarters triggers statutory accountability; a single month's breach is different. Benefits: anchor expectations, transparency, protect real returns and reduce inflation uncertainty. Limits: supply shocks, monetary-transmission lags and growth costs of excessive tightening.

## Control: match the policy to the cause

![A rate rise restrains demand](Revision%20Diagrams/policy.svg)

| Policy | Instruments | Limitation / trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Monetary | Raise repo/SDF rates, absorb liquidity via OMO sales, adjust CRR; selective credit controls/moral suasion | Restrains demand and second-round effects; cannot directly produce onions/oil |
| Fiscal | Restrain excess demand, reprioritise expenditure, targeted relief; tax/duty adjustment | Broad contraction can hurt employment/capex; tax rises may raise costs |
| Supply / administrative | Buffers, imports, lower logistics losses, anti-hoarding action, temporary stock/export measures | Export bans hurt producers; blanket controls can distort incentives |
| Structural | Irrigation, storage/cold chains, productivity, diversified imports and competitive markets | Takes time; most important for persistent bottlenecks |

SDF has been the liquidity-corridor floor since 2022; do not mechanically describe fixed reverse repo as the current floor. SLR/bank rate are textbook instruments but not interchangeable with the operating repo rate. Countercyclical government taxation/spending is **fiscal**, not qualitative monetary policy.

**Food-inflation answer:** identify climate/yield, seasonality, oil/feed/fertiliser, protein-demand changes and storage/marketing bottlenecks → RBI anchors expectations and limits spillovers → government tackles supply → protect vulnerable households without fuelling broad demand.

## Indian measures and dated examples

- **Essential Commodities Act, 1955** and **Prevention of Blackmarketing and Maintenance of Supplies of Essential Commodities Act, 1980**: legal tools against shortages/hoarding, subject to lawful notification and safeguards.
- Price Stabilisation Fund buffers; OMSS wheat/rice releases; Bharat atta/rice/dal; pulse/onion imports and temporary duty or export adjustments.
- Operation Greens began with **TOP (tomato, onion, potato)** and was expanded to 41 perishables; Kisan Rail and cold-chain investment improve distribution. GST can reduce tax cascading, but not every GST change reduces prices.
- Source's wheat stock limits (24 June 2024-31 March 2025), pulse stock/import measures (2024-25), onion buffer/export-duty measures (2024) and 2021-22 buffer quantities are **historical examples**, not continuing deadlines.
- **Economic Survey 2025-26:** April-December 2025 average headline inflation **1.7%**, a partial-year figure in the then prevailing CPI series. [Economic Survey release](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2220004&lang=1&reg=6).
- **January 2026 CPI:** initially 2.75% provisional, revised to **2.74% final** on the new 2024 base. Never compare index levels across rebased series directly. [MoSPI February release](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2238889&lang=2&reg=48).

## PYQ revision cues

| Year(s) | Correct idea |
|---|---|
| 2023 | Rate hikes combat consumer inflation through monetary policy; OMO is a sterilisation instrument |
| 2022 | RBI maintains price stability; sell dollars against rapid rupee depreciation; buy dollars can absorb incoming forex |
| 2021 | Expansionary policy + fiscal stimulus + purchasing power can drive demand-pull inflation |
| 2020 | CPI food weight exceeds WPI's in the questioned series; CPI includes services, WPI does not; RBI did not switch from CPI to WPI |
| 2015 | CPI-IW compiler = Labour Bureau; reduced money circulation can restrain inflation |
| 2013 | Unexpected inflation benefits debtors; money/demand rise and output fall can raise prices; creating money to finance deficit is especially inflationary |
| 2011 | Base effect concerns the previous comparison-period price level; food demand and structural supply constraints matter |
| 2010 | Deflation = persistent general price decline; the WPI frequency question is historical |

**Mains 2024:** causes of persistent food inflation and limits/effectiveness of RBI policy. **Mains 2019:** judge GDP growth and low inflation alongside jobs, investment, distribution, credit and external/fiscal risks; two indicators alone do not establish economic health.
